Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Actions on Objectives
Likely
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Corporate endpoint browsing the ascarding.net carding forum · [LLM] Internal host connecting to NetNut / Alarum residential-proxy infrastructure · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Corporate endpoint browsing the ascarding.net carding forum AICommand & Control High
Hunts internal hosts resolving or connecting to ascarding.net ("The Carding Forum Asylum"), the forum hosting the 'Getting the Cleanest Possible IPs for Carding' guide central to this Flare report. Near-zero legitimate business reason for a corporate device to reach a carding marketplace, making it a high-fidelity insider-fraud / compromised-host signal. Rationale: Uses the exact carding-forum domain ascarding.net named/screenshotted in the article and confirmed via search as 'The Carding Forum Asylum' hosting the cited carding guide; corporate endpoints have virtually no legitimate reason to reach it, so it is high-fidelity with minimal enumeration. Cross-checked against: • https://ascarding.net/threads/3970/ • https://ascarding.net/forums/44/
ATT&CKT1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intelligence analyst manually browsing the forum from a sanctioned research workstation
  • SOC analyst validating an IOC during triage
  • Malware sandbox / detonation VM following a URL from a feed
  • Security-vendor crawler running on corporate egress
  • User clicking an ascarding.net link embedded in a phishing/threat-report email
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName in~ ("ti-research-vm01","soc-sandbox01") or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-tithreatintel"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the device, user and initiating process (browser vs. non-browser/automation). Confirm the host is not a sanctioned TI/research asset and the account is not a security analyst. 2) Contain: if the device is a standard corporate endpoint, isolate it, force credential reset for the user, and block ascarding.net at the proxy/DNS. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for connections to netnut.com/netnut.io/alarum.io and other proxy vendors, antidetect-browser installs (e.g. Dolphin, GoLogin, Multilogin), and any access to internal payment/finance systems in the surrounding window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "ascarding.net"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has "ascarding.net"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by FirstSeen desc
title: Endpoint DNS/Web Access to ascarding.net Carding Forum
id: 6f3b9a12-4c2e-4d7a-9f11-2a7c8e6b1d04
description: Detects a host resolving or connecting to ascarding.net, a known carding forum central to the Flare residential-proxy carding report.
references:
  - https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/inside-the-search-for-clean-residential-proxies-for-carding/
  - https://ascarding.net/threads/3970/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/17
tags:

  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    query|contains: 'ascarding.net'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationHostname:(*ascarding.net* OR *ASCARDING.NET*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/ascarding\.net/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_host="*ascarding.net*" OR All_Traffic.url="*ascarding.net*" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_host="*ascarding.net*" OR All_Traffic.url="*ascarding.net*" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.user All_Traffic.app | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Internal host connecting to NetNut / Alarum residential-proxy infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts corporate devices resolving or connecting to netnut.com, netnut.io or alarum.io — the residential-proxy vendor (Alarum Technologies / NetNut) whose exit nodes the FBI seized in July 2026 and which carders in this report seek for 'clean' finance-compatible IPs. A device reaching these gateways typically indicates residential-proxy client software running locally to anonymize/geo-shift outbound sessions. Rationale: Uses the four concrete vendor domains named in the article (netnut.com, netnut.io, alarum.io) corroborated by the FBI/Google NetNut-Popa seizure; DNS to these gateways from an endpoint is a strong indicator of residential-proxy client tooling rather than incidental browsing. Cross-checked against: • https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/07/fbi-seizes-netnut-proxy-platform-popa-botnet/ • https://www.infosecurity-magazine.com/news/fbi-google-take-down-netnut-proxy/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/netnut-proxy-network-disrupted-2-million-infected-devices-cut-off/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1090.003
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Marketing / ad-verification team legitimately licensing NetNut for localized ad checks
  • Brand-protection or SEO tooling using residential proxies for geo testing
  • QA/localization team validating region-specific site rendering
  • Threat-intel analyst visiting the vendor site post-seizure to review the takedown
  • Security researcher enumerating proxy vendors from a sandbox
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName startswith "mktg-" or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-adverify","svc-brandprotect"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: determine which process reached the domain (a browser tab to the marketing site is far lower risk than a headless/service binary hitting a gateway API). Check whether the user/device belongs to a sanctioned marketing or research function. 2) Contain: for non-sanctioned hosts, isolate the endpoint, hunt for and remove residential-proxy client binaries, and block netnut.com/netnut.io/alarum.io at DNS/proxy. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/user with ascarding.net access, antidetect-browser artefacts, and abnormal logins to internal finance/payment portals or customer PII stores in the surrounding window.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io","alarum.io")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(), Urls=make_set(RemoteUrl,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by FirstSeen desc
DnsEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Name has_any ("netnut.com","netnut.io","alarum.io")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType
| order by FirstSeen desc

Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] serverValidation.js loader executed by Node from trojanized coding-test repo
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Node.js runtime beaconing to REF9403 rightwidth.dev Socket.IO C2 · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] OtterCookie file stealer reading AI coding-assistant config dirs (.claude/.cursor/.windsurf) · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Node.js runtime beaconing to REF9403 rightwidth.dev Socket.IO C2 AICommand & Control High
Hunts a node.exe/npm process resolving or connecting to the REF9403 command-and-control infrastructure (ldb/upload/controller.rightwidth.dev) used by the OtterCookie-aligned four-stage payload. Node is not a browser, so an interpreter reaching this dev-TLD domain family is a high-fidelity C2 signal specific to the fake-coding-test lure. Rationale: Anchors on the four confirmed C2 subdomains (ldb/upload/controller.rightwidth.dev) plus a node/npm initiator so it fires on interpreter-driven C2 even though the domain is single-sourced to Elastic; a JS runtime resolving a dev-TLD attacker domain is near-zero in benign traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/ • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/03/11/contagious-interview-malware-delivered-through-fake-developer-job-interviews/ • https://cyberandramen.net/2026/04/04/ottercookie-expands-targeting-to-ai-coding-tools-analysis-of-a-trojanized-npm-campaign/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer legitimately using a package or SaaS hosted on a *.rightwidth.dev subdomain (validate the specific FQDN against the IOC list)
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a sanctioned analysis VM
  • Corporate proxy/DNS-sinkhole re-resolving the domain for blocking (resolver IP, not endpoint)
  • Threat-intel feed enrichment tooling actively resolving IOCs
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl == "rightwidth.dev" and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("threatintel","ioc-check","sandbox"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the resolving process is node/npm and pull InitiatingProcessCommandLine to find the trojanized repo path; check whether the host cloned a repo referencing Next.js v14/NestJS/Auth.js lure stack. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block *.rightwidth.dev at DNS/proxy, and kill the node process tree; preserve the repo and node_modules for forensics. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same aid/DeviceName for reads of .claude/.cursor/.windsurf dirs, browser Login Data, and crypto-wallet extension storage, and rotate any credentials/AI-service tokens present on the host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "rightwidth.dev" or RemoteUrl in~ ("ldb.rightwidth.dev","upload.rightwidth.dev","controller.rightwidth.dev","rightwidth.dev")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.cmd","npm","yarn.cmd","electron.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery endswith "rightwidth.dev"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OtterCookie file stealer reading AI coding-assistant config dirs (.claude/.cursor/.windsurf) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts a Node.js process enumerating the AI coding-tool configuration directories (.claude, .cursor, .gemini, .windsurf, .pearai, .llama) that OtterCookie's file-stealer module explicitly harvests for API keys, tokens and LLM conversation logs. This directory set touched by a JS interpreter is the novel differentiator in the REF9403 campaign. Rationale: Uses the exact six AI-tool config dir names OtterCookie enumerates (corroborated by Talos and cyberandramen.net) with a node.exe initiator; a JS runtime crawling .claude/.cursor/.windsurf together is behaviour no legitimate build tool exhibits. Cross-checked against: • https://cyberandramen.net/2026/04/04/ottercookie-expands-targeting-to-ai-coding-tools-analysis-of-a-trojanized-npm-campaign/ • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.001 T1119
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • The AI tools themselves updating their config (initiating process is cursor.exe/claude.exe, not node.exe)
  • A developer's own dotfile-sync or backup script running under node reading these dirs
  • VS Code extensions built on Node performing legitimate config reads of a single tool
  • Security tooling inventorying installed AI extensions
Suppression filter
| where DirsTouched >= 2 and InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "dotfiles-sync"
Response runbook
1) Triage: inspect InitiatingProcessCommandLine — legitimate access reads one tool dir; OtterCookie sweeps all six plus .env/.pem/.key/.ssh. Confirm the parent is an npm-launched project, not the AI IDE. 2) Contain: isolate host, suspend the node process, and immediately rotate all AI-service API tokens (Claude/Cursor/Gemini) and any secrets found in the swept directories. 3) Hunt: correlate with rightwidth.dev C2 (UC1) and serverValidation.js execution (UC3) on the same host, and check for browser Login Data / crypto-wallet extension reads.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FolderPath has_any ("\\.claude\\","\\.cursor\\","\\.gemini\\","\\.windsurf\\","\\.pearai\\","\\.llama\\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FileCount=dcount(FileName), DirsTouched=make_set(FolderPath, 10), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where TargetFilePath has_any ("\\.claude\\","\\.cursor\\","\\.gemini\\","\\.windsurf\\","\\.pearai\\","\\.llama\\")
| summarize FileCount=dcount(TargetFilePath), Dirs=make_set(TargetFilePath, 10), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Node.js Process Accessing AI Coding-Assistant Config Directories (OtterCookie)

| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Filesystem.file_path) as file_paths dc(Filesystem.file_name) as distinct_files min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\.claude\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.cursor\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.gemini\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.windsurf\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.pearai\\*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*\\.llama\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=inner process_guid [| tstats summariesonly=false values(Processes.process_name) as process_name from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("node.exe","node") by Processes.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`] | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | sort - lastTime
serverValidation.js loader executed by Node from trojanized coding-test repo AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the OtterCookie loader serverValidation.js, which reassembles the base64 payload fragments hidden in HTML comments across the country-flag SVG images (AE.svg, AF.svg) in the repo's assets directory. Detection targets the named loader script running under node as part of the fake coding-assessment repo. Rationale: Uses the exact loader filename serverValidation.js named by Elastic plus a node interpreter; dual proc+filewrite Defender coverage catches both cmdline-visible and require()-loaded execution, so the detection survives whether the script is passed as an arg or imported. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/north-korea-linked-hackers-hide.html • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/beavertail-and-ottercookie/
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027.003 T1195.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate project genuinely shipping an unrelated file named serverValidation.js (verify repo origin and whether it reads SVG assets)
  • Developer authoring server-side validation logic in a file coincidentally named the same
  • CI/CD pipeline running a benign validation step under node
Response runbook
1) Triage: locate the parent repo dir, inspect the assets/ folder for country-flag SVGs (AE.svg, AF.svg) containing base64 in HTML comments, and read serverValidation.js for base64 reassembly/eval logic. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the node tree, quarantine the repo, and block rightwidth.dev. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same repo/loader across other developer endpoints (Slack-lure victims), and pivot to UC1 C2 beacons and UC2 AI-config-dir reads; rotate credentials on any confirmed host.
union
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ ("node.exe","node") and ProcessCommandLine has "serverValidation.js"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Signal="proc", InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath ),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "serverValidation.js"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, Signal="filewrite", InitiatingProcessFileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FolderPath )
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "serverValidation.js"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc

| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,

Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy

Unit 42 (Palo Alto)
2026-07-17 8 use cases 3 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A technical analysis of three chained zero-day vulnerabilities in Siemens ROX II OT switches that allow privilege escalation and persistent root access. The post Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy appeared first on Unit 42 .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II xz-as-cat arbitrary disclosure of shadow/private keys (CVE-2025-40948) · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II feature-key gpgv command injection to root (CVE-2025-40947) · [LLM] Siemens ROX II three-stage zero-day chain temporal correlation (CVE-2025-40948/40947/40949) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Siemens ROX II root cron persistence via web task scheduler (CVE-2025-40949) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Three Steps to the Terminal: A Siemens ROX II Zero-Day Trilogy
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Siemens ROX II xz-as-cat arbitrary disclosure of shadow/private keys (CVE-2025-40948) AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the CVE-2025-40948 stage where a root-privileged xz utility is misused with decompress-to-stdout flags to read sensitive files (/etc/shadow, SSH/TLS private keys, config) on a Ruggedcom ROX II OT switch. Article-specific: xz functioning like cat against credential-bearing files is the reconnaissance foothold of the chain. Rationale: Uses the article's exact CVE-2025-40948 mechanic — root-privileged xz used like cat (decompress-to-stdout) against password hashes and private keys. Pairing xz with a sensitive-file target and a stdout/decompress flag makes it high-fidelity; xz legitimately never streams /etc/shadow. Cross-checked NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02 • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/siemens-rox-ii-zero-day-vulnerabilities/
ATT&CKT1003.008 T1552.004 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin decompressing a .xz log/backup archive with xz -dc to a pager
  • Firmware/update tooling that pipes xz -d output during a package install
  • A monitoring script that reads a config file that happens to end in .key but is not a private key
  • Backup jobs streaming compressed archives from /etc via xz
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("backup","firmware","/var/log/") and not SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/shadow","id_rsa","id_dsa","ssl/private"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full Syslog/auditd EXECVE line — confirm the xz target is /etc/shadow, an SSH/TLS private key, or a credential config, and identify the invoking user/session on the ROX II switch. 2) Contain: isolate the switch's management plane (block untrusted access to the web/CLI mgmt VLAN), rotate any exposed device keys/passwords, and confirm firmware is upgraded to V2.17.1. 3) Hunt: on the same device look for the follow-on chain — feature-key command injection (CVE-2025-40947) and root crontab modification (CVE-2025-40949) within the following minutes.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ProcessName has "xz" or SyslogMessage has "xz"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/etc/shadow","id_rsa","id_dsa","ssl/private",".pem",".key")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("--decompress","-dc"," -d ","--stdout","-c ")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage, Facility, SeverityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Siemens ROX II feature-key gpgv command injection to root (CVE-2025-40947) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts CVE-2025-40947: an attacker-controlled feature-key payload submitted to the ROX II web/CLI management is inserted unsanitized into a root-privileged command, allowing shell command injection. Article-specific: feature-key validation input carrying shell metacharacters is the privilege-escalation pivot of the chain. Rationale: Grounded in the CVE-2025-40947 description — an unsanitized feature-key payload inserted directly into a root command. Detecting shell metacharacters (;, |, &&, $(), backtick, $IFS) inside a feature-key request/log line is high-fidelity because a legitimate feature key is an opaque signed token with no shell syntax. Corroborated via NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1548
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin pasting a legitimate feature key that coincidentally contains a semicolon-delimited field
  • WAF/proxy URL-decoding artifacts that surface encoded characters in benign query strings
  • Automated inventory tooling querying the feature-key endpoint without injection payloads
  • Penetration-test / vulnerability-scanner traffic fuzzing the mgmt interface
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("scanner","nessus","qualys") or ProcessName has_any ("nessus","scan"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: reconstruct the feature-key request/log entry — confirm shell metacharacters are inside the attacker-controlled key field rather than a benign token, and identify the authenticated user and source IP. 2) Contain: revoke the session, restrict the ROX II management interface to a trusted jump host, and verify firmware V2.17.1 is applied (the fix). 3) Hunt: check for a preceding CVE-2025-40948 xz file read and a following CVE-2025-40949 root crontab write on the same device to confirm full-chain execution; capture any commands spawned as root.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where SyslogMessage has "feature" and SyslogMessage has "key"
| where SyslogMessage contains "$(" or SyslogMessage contains "&&" or SyslogMessage contains "`" or SyslogMessage contains ";" or SyslogMessage contains "| " or SyslogMessage contains "$IFS"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, SyslogMessage, Facility, SeverityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:linux.syslog "feature-key" (";sh" OR "&&" OR "|sh" OR "|bash" OR "$IFS" OR "; /")

Siemens ROX II root cron persistence via web task scheduler (CVE-2025-40949) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts CVE-2025-40949: an authenticated attacker abuses the ROX II web management task scheduler to inject commands into the root crontab, establishing reboot-surviving persistence. Article-specific: new root cron entries executing network-fetch or /tmp payloads are the persistence stage of the chain. Rationale: Maps to the CVE-2025-40949 mechanic — injected commands in the root cron table via the web scheduler. Cron parentage plus a remote-fetch/shell payload is high-fidelity: legitimate ROX II cron jobs do not curl/wget from /tmp or spawn reverse shells. Corroborated via NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02
ATT&CKT1053.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate scheduled maintenance job that uses curl/wget to pull an update from an internal server
  • Vendor diagnostic cron task writing to /tmp
  • Admin-created backup cron entry piping data out via a shell
  • Config-management agent (e.g. an internal orchestration script) launched from cron
Suppression filter
| where not (SyslogMessage has_any ("/opt/siemens/","internal-update") and RemoteHostAllowlisted == true)
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the current root crontab and the ROX II task-scheduler audit entry — confirm the offending job was created via the web scheduler and points at an external host or /tmp payload. 2) Contain: remove the malicious cron entry, kill any spawned payload process, isolate the switch's mgmt plane, and upgrade to firmware V2.17.1. 3) Hunt: correlate backward to the CVE-2025-40947 feature-key injection and CVE-2025-40948 xz disclosure on the same device, and sweep other ROX II switches for identical cron entries or callback destinations.
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility =~ "cron" or ProcessName has_any ("crontab","crond","CRON")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("wget","curl","/tmp/","bash -i","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d","nc ") or SyslogMessage contains "$("
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, ProcessName, Facility, SyslogMessage, SeverityLevel
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Siemens ROX II three-stage zero-day chain temporal correlation (CVE-2025-40948/40947/40949) AIExploitation High
Correlates the three chained ROX II exploit stages — xz file disclosure, feature-key command injection, and root cron persistence — observed on the same switch within a short window. Article-specific: alerts on the documented 'three steps to the terminal' progression rather than any single stage in isolation. Rationale: Encodes the article's core thesis — the 'three steps to the terminal' chain — by requiring ≥2 distinct documented stages (xz disclosure, feature-key injection, root cron persistence) on one ROX II switch within a 10-minute bin, which is far higher-fidelity than any single-stage alert. Datadog query surfaces the indicators; the count/window is applied at rule level. Corroborated via NVD and CISA ICSA-26-134-02. Cross-checked against: • https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-40947 • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/ics-advisories/icsa-26-134-02
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004 T1053.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized penetration test replaying the full chain against a lab ROX II
  • Vendor validation run of the V2.17.1 patch that exercises xz, feature-key and scheduler code paths
  • Noisy vulnerability scanner touching all three mgmt endpoints in one sweep
  • A single benign admin session that legitimately reads a config, sets a feature key, and edits a cron job in quick succession
Suppression filter
| where not (Computer has_any ("lab","test","staging") or HostIP in ("127.0.0.1"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the correlated evidence set and confirm the stages are attacker-driven (sensitive-file xz read, metacharacters in feature-key, remote/tmp cron payload) rather than benign admin work; identify the switch, user and source IP. 2) Contain: isolate the switch management plane, revoke the session, remove any malicious cron entry, rotate exposed device credentials/keys, and enforce firmware V2.17.1. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source IP and callback destinations across all ROX II / Ruggedcom devices for identical chain activity and stage-3 persistence artifacts.
let Window = 10m;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| extend Stage = case(
    SyslogMessage has "xz" and SyslogMessage has_any("/etc/shadow","id_rsa","id_dsa","ssl/private",".pem",".key"), "1-disclosure",
    (SyslogMessage has "feature" and SyslogMessage has "key") and (SyslogMessage contains "$(" or SyslogMessage contains "&&" or SyslogMessage contains ";" or SyslogMessage contains "`" or SyslogMessage contains "$IFS"), "2-cmdinjection",
    (ProcessName has_any ("cron","crond","crontab") or Facility =~ "cron") and (SyslogMessage has_any("wget","curl","/tmp/","/dev/tcp/","base64 -d") or SyslogMessage contains "$("), "3-persistence",
    "")
| where isnotempty(Stage)
| summarize Stages = make_set(Stage), StageCount = dcount(Stage), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Evidence = make_list(SyslogMessage, 20) by Computer, HostIP, bin(TimeGenerated, Window)
| where StageCount >= 2   // >=2 of the 3 documented stages on one switch inside a 10m bin
| order by LastSeen desc

ACR Stealer Uses ClickFix Lures to Steal Browser Tokens and Microsoft 365 Files

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 19 use cases 8 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

ACR Stealer, an infostealer in circulation since 2024, is walking out of enterprise networks with saved browser passwords, live session tokens, PDFs, Microsoft 365 documents, and files from synced OneDrive and SharePoint folders. It gets in because someone pasted a command into a Run box and pressed Enter. Microsoft laid out two of the delivery chains on Thursday. Its Defender Experts team, the

Exploitation. ClickFix Run-dialog paste writes mshta/rundll32/pushd command to Explorer RunMRU AIDelivery High
Hunts the ClickFix initial-access step where a victim pastes an attacker-supplied command into the Windows Run box; the shell records it under HKCU\...\Explorer\RunMRU. Fires when that recorded command contains the LOLBins ACR Stealer's chains use (mshta, rundll32, pushd, conhost) or a remote/UNC target. Rationale: RunMRU is the definitive fingerprint of a Run-box paste, and pairing it with the article's exact LOLBins (mshta, rundll32, pushd, conhost) plus a remote/UNC target makes it ClickFix-specific rather than generic autorun noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://isc.sans.edu/diary/33018 • https://www.lindensec.com/post/dissecting-a-live-clickfix-attack-etherhiding-webdav-abuse-and-how-asr-saves-the-day
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power users legitimately launching cmd/powershell from the Run box for admin work
  • IT scripts distributed by helpdesk telling users to paste a benign diagnostic command
  • Software vendors documenting a 'paste this into Run' install workaround
  • Automated GPO/logon scripts that seed RunMRU on imaged machines
  • Developers testing rundll32/mshta invocations locally
Suppression filter
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("\\\\","http://","https://","mshta","rundll32","pushd","conhost") and not (RegistryValueData has_any ("\\\\corp\\","\\\\dfs\\") and InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe" and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("helpdesk","svc-imaging"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full RegistryValueData and resolve any http/UNC target; check whether the same host then spawned mshta.exe or rundll32.exe within minutes (join DeviceProcessEvents on DeviceId). 2) Contain: if a remote HTA or WebDAV DLL load followed, isolate the host, kill mshta/rundll32/pythonw, and revoke the signed-in user's session tokens (not just password). 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the same RunMRU string and for outbound connections to the ACR campaign domains; check for the pythonw.exe/scheduled-task persistence artifacts.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "RegistryValueSet"
| where RegistryKey has @"\Explorer\RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("mshta","rundll32","powershell","pwsh","pushd","conhost","curl","http","\\\\")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Explorer\RunMRU"
| where RegistryValueData has_any ("mshta","rundll32","powershell","pwsh","pushd","conhost","curl","http","\\")
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

mshta.exe fileless chain: remote HTA fetch then in-memory PowerShell with TLS-validation bypass AIExploitation High
Hunts ACR Stealer's fileless chain where the pasted command spawns mshta.exe to pull remote HTA content, whose VBScript loader fires PowerShell that disables certificate validation and runs a JPEG-carried payload in memory. Anchors on mshta.exe invoking a remote URL/.hta and flags the .NET cert-bypass strings when present. Rationale: mshta.exe fetching a remote HTA is the documented fileless entry point; the cert-bypass strings (ServicePointManager.ServerCertificateValidationCallback) are searched inside ProcessCommandLine as enrichment, not treated as schema columns, fixing the prior validation error. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://isc.sans.edu/diary/33018
ATT&CKT1218.005 T1059.001 T1027.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legacy internal LOB apps still delivered as HTA from an intranet URL
  • Vendor tooling that shells mshta against an internal http endpoint
  • Admin troubleshooting scripts using mshta with a local file (excluded by http/.hta filter)
  • Security-tool self-tests / atomic red team runs
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://intranet","https://intranet",".corp.local") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("iexplore.exe","explorer.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the remote URL, resolve it, and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the follow-on JPEG pull from an image host; look for a PowerShell child of this mshta with the cert-bypass strings. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate mshta/powershell, and revoke the user's browser session tokens since credential theft runs in-memory. 3) Hunt: pivot on the image-host domain and on any host that resolved it; check for Chrome/Edge 'Login Data'/'Web Data' access by non-browser processes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "mshta.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://",".hta")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend CertBypass = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ServerCertificateValidationCallback","CheckCertificateRevocation","ServicePointManager")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, CertBypass
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://","https://",".hta")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| extend CertBypass = CommandLine has_any ("ServerCertificateValidationCallback","CheckCertificateRevocation","ServicePointManager")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, CertBypass
| order by TimeGenerated desc

rundll32.exe loading a DLL from a WebDAV/UNC share by ordinal export AIInstallation High
Hunts the disk-leaving ACR Stealer chain that runs rundll32.exe against a DLL pulled from a remote WebDAV share (GUID directory, fake extension like .google) and invoked by ordinal (,#1). Matches rundll32 with a UNC path plus an ordinal-export invocation, and the named host sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net. Rationale: rundll32 loading a DLL by ordinal from a UNC/WebDAV path is exactly Red Canary's / Microsoft's documented example command; the ordinal-export regex plus the named host sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net make this high-fidelity and low-FP. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/intelligence-insights-may-2026/ • https://isc.sans.edu/diary/33018
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1570 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise software that legitimately runs a DLL from a signed internal DFS/UNC share
  • Deployment tooling (SCCM/Intune) invoking rundll32 against a network path
  • Printer/driver installers referencing UNC resources
  • Backup/AV agents loading helper DLLs from a mapped drive
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\\\corp\\","\\\\dfs.","\\\\fileserver") and InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","msiexec.exe","services.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the UNC host in the command line; confirm it is external (not a corp DFS/file server) and check DeviceNetworkEvents for the WebDAV connection over 443. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the remote host at proxy/firewall, terminate rundll32, and revoke the user's tokens. 3) Hunt: search for the same GUID-directory pattern and fake extensions (.google/.ct) org-wide, plus pushd usage mounting a remote share and conhost.exe --headless wrappers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "\\\\"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i),\s*#?\d+"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| extend NamedHost = ProcessCommandLine has_any ("sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net",".google,",".ct,")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, NamedHost
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe"
| where CommandLine contains "\\\\"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i),\s*#?\d+"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: b7d40e19-3c8a-4f52-9e21-0a6d5c8f13be
status: experimental
description: Detects rundll32.exe invoked against a UNC/WebDAV path with an ordinal export, matching ACR Stealer's disk-based chain (e.g. sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net GUID dir, google.ct payload).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/acr-stealer-uses-clickfix-lures-to.html
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/17
tags:
  - attack.t1218.011
  - attack.t1570
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\rundll32.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '\\\\'
  selection_ordinal:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - ',#1'
      - ',#'
  condition: selection and selection_ordinal
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\rundll32.exe OR *\\RUNDLL32.EXE) @CommandLine:*\\\\* @CommandLine:(*,#1* OR *,\ #1* OR *sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net* OR *.google,* OR *.ct,*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\rundll32\.exe$/i
| regex("\\\\\\\\[^ ]+,\\s*#?\\d+", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=rundll32.exe Processes.process="*\\\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="(?i),\s*#?\d+" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=rundll32.exe Processes.process="*\\\\*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="(?i),\s*#?\d+" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
conhost.exe --headless wrapping pushd/rundll32 (ClickFix console-hiding variant) AIInstallation High
Hunts the stealthiest ACR Stealer variant that wraps its WebDAV rundll32 execution in conhost.exe --headless to suppress the console window, mounting the remote share with pushd and hiding strings behind delayed environment-variable expansion. Anchors on the rare conhost --headless flag alongside pushd/rundll32/UNC content. Rationale: conhost.exe --headless is an uncommon flag that Microsoft specifically calls out as the stealthiest ACR variant's console-hiding trick; pairing it with pushd/rundll32/UNC content in the same or parent command line removes benign headless-console noise. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://www.cyberproof.com/blog/the-clickfix-evolution-new-variant-replaces-powershell-with-rundll32-and-webdav/
ATT&CKT1564.003 T1218.011 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Windows Terminal / modern console host spawning conhost with new flags during updates
  • Developer tooling invoking conhost --headless for pseudo-console (ConPTY) automation
  • CI/build agents using headless consoles
  • Terminal-emulator apps embedding conhost
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("windowsterminal.exe","wt.exe","code.exe","devenv.exe") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the parent command line and expand any delayed-expansion (%var%) strings to reveal the hidden pushd/rundll32/host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the conhost/rundll32 tree, and revoke the user's session tokens. 3) Hunt: search for pushd mounting remote shares, the WebDAV DLL-load pattern, and follow-on pythonw.exe execution from %LocalAppData%\Temp on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "conhost.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "--headless"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pushd","rundll32","cmd","\\\\") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pushd","rundll32","--headless")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\conhost.exe"
| where CommandLine has "--headless"
| where CommandLine has_any ("pushd","rundll32","cmd","\\\\")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: conhost.exe --headless Launching pushd/rundll32
id: e51a9d76-6c22-4b8f-9a04-3f7e2c1b8d90

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=conhost.exe Processes.process="*--headless*" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | search process="*pushd*" OR process="*rundll32*" OR process="*\\\\*" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
pythonw.exe silently running a script from %LocalAppData%\Temp (LogiOptionsPlus lure) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the second-stage ACR loader: obfuscated PowerShell drops a ZIP into a folder under %LocalAppData%\Temp with an innocuous name (e.g. LogiOptionsPlus) and a bundled pythonw.exe launches the Python script so nothing appears on screen. Anchors on pythonw.exe running a .py from an AppData\Local\Temp path spawned by a script host. Rationale: pythonw.exe (no console) running a script out of %LocalAppData%\Temp under an innocuous folder name and spawned by PowerShell is the exact stealthy loader Microsoft describes; LogiOptionsPlus is the named decoy folder used as a strong anchor. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://www.lindensec.com/post/dissecting-a-live-clickfix-attack-etherhiding-webdav-abuse-and-how-asr-saves-the-day
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1204.002 T1564.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Python apps that bundle pythonw and run scripts from a per-user temp/cache dir
  • Data-science tooling launching pythonw from AppData
  • Packaged Electron/Python installers unpacking to Temp on first run
  • Developer venv activity under the user profile
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","conda.exe","code.exe") or FolderPath has_any ("\\Programs\\Python\\","\\Anaconda3\\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: locate the .py path and the parent ZIP under %LocalAppData%\Temp; confirm the parent was obfuscated PowerShell, and check whether the installer wiped prior copies (updater behavior). 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate pythonw, remove the scheduled task, and revoke tokens. 3) Hunt: look for the second Python loader making outbound connections to blockchain RPC/Web3 endpoints (EtherHiding) and for the timestomp/PS-history-clear persistence markers.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pythonw.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".py","LogiOptionsPlus")
| where FolderPath has @"\AppData\Local\" or ProcessCommandLine has @"AppData\Local\Temp" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\pythonw.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any (".py","LogiOptionsPlus")
| where CommandLine has @"AppData\Local\Temp" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: pythonw.exe Running Script From LocalAppData Temp
id: c9f2a1b8-7e34-4d6c-8b90-5a1e3f0c72d4
status: experimental

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=pythonw.exe (Processes.process="*.py*" OR Processes.process="*LogiOptionsPlus*") (Processes.process="*AppData\\Local\\Temp*" OR Processes.parent_process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.parent_process_name=pwsh.exe) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Hidden scheduled task masquerading as a software update, created by a script host AIInstallation Medium
Hunts ACR Stealer's persistence: a hidden scheduled task posing as a software update, created not by a legitimate installer but by powershell/python/cmd. Anchors on schtasks.exe /create with update-themed task names and a script-host or pythonw parent. Rationale: The differentiator from benign updaters is the parent: legit update tasks are registered by installers/services, not by powershell/python/mshta/rundll32; combined with update-themed naming this isolates ACR's masquerading persistence. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admins scripting scheduled-task creation via PowerShell for genuine patch jobs
  • Configuration-management tools (Ansible/DSC) that create update tasks from a shell
  • Third-party updater frameworks that self-register via a wrapper script
  • Software packaging during app deployment
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("Ansible","DesiredStateConfiguration","Intune") or InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-patch","svc-sccm"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the task's action (schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml) to reveal the payload path — check for pythonw/rundll32 and hidden window flags. 2) Contain: delete the task, isolate the host, terminate the payload process, and revoke user tokens. 3) Hunt: correlate with timestamp copying off notepad.exe (timestomp) and Microsoft-PowerShell/Operational history clearing on the same host, and sweep the org for identically named tasks.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("update","Update","LogiOptions","OneDrive")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","pythonw.exe","python.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create"
| where CommandLine has_any ("update","Update","LogiOptions","OneDrive")
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","pythonw.exe","python.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Scheduled Task Masquerading as Software Update Created by Script Host
id: a2e7f4c0-1b93-4d8e-8f21-6c0a9d3b57e2
status: experimental
description: Detects schtasks.exe /create using update-themed task names spawned by powershell/python/mshta/rundll32, matching ACR Stealer persistence.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/acr-stealer-uses-clickfix-lures-to.html
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/17
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: '/create'
  selection_name:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'update'
      - 'LogiOptions'
      - 'OneDrive'
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
      - '\pythonw.exe'
      - '\python.exe'
      - '\mshta.exe'
      - '\rundll32.exe'
  condition: selection and selection_name and selection_parent
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:*/create* @CommandLine:(*update* OR *Update* OR *LogiOptions*) @ParentImage:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\pwsh.exe OR *\\pythonw.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\mshta.exe OR *\\rundll32.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i
| regex("/create", field=CommandLine)
| regex("(update|LogiOptions|OneDrive)", field=CommandLine, flags="i")
| ParentBaseFileName=/(powershell|pwsh|python|pythonw|mshta|rundll32)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe Processes.process="*/create*" (Processes.process="*update*" OR Processes.process="*Update*" OR Processes.process="*LogiOptions*") (Processes.parent_process_name=powershell.exe OR Processes.parent_process_name=pwsh.exe OR Processes.parent_process_name=cmd.exe OR Processes.parent_process_name=pythonw.exe OR Processes.parent_process_name=python.exe) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Python loader making EtherHiding calls to blockchain RPC / Web3 node infrastructure AICommand & Control Low
Hunts the EtherHiding C2 stage where a second Python loader queries public blockchain RPC endpoints / Web3 node infrastructure to pull a payload or C2 address off a public ledger. Anchors on python/pythonw.exe reaching public Web3/RPC hosts — no attacker-controlled resolver to seize, so process-to-blockchain egress is the signal. Rationale: Microsoft explicitly names EtherHiding via a second Python loader talking to public blockchain RPC/Web3 nodes; the article gives no fixed domains, so this is scoped to python(w).exe reaching Web3/RPC hostnames and shipped as Low-confidence hunting — validate hits against the campaign process tree. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/clickfix-campaign-uses-etherhiding-and-guloader/
ATT&CKT1102 T1071.001 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate blockchain/crypto developers running Python Web3 clients (web3.py) on corporate hosts
  • Data engineers pulling on-chain data via python scripts
  • Trading/analytics tools that query public RPC nodes
  • Wallet or dApp automation on developer workstations
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("\\Programs\\Python\\","\\Anaconda3\\","\\venv\\") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "web3.py")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating pythonw.exe came from %LocalAppData%\Temp (not a dev venv) and correlate with the ClickFix process tree on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate python(w), and treat the user's tokens/creds as compromised (revoke, not rotate). 3) Hunt: capture the RPC hostname/contract queried, block it, and check whether the resolved payload/C2 led to browser credential-store access or M365 file collection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pythonw.exe","python.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("rpc","web3","infura","alchemy","ankr","bsc-dataseed","mainnet","binance","polygon-rpc","eth")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Dvc has_any ("") or true
| where tostring(DstHostname) has_any ("rpc","web3","infura","alchemy","ankr","bsc-dataseed","mainnet","binance","polygon-rpc")
| where SrcUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, DstHostname, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @Image:(*\\pythonw.exe OR *\\python.exe OR *\\PYTHONW.EXE) @DestinationHostname:(*rpc* OR *web3* OR *infura* OR *alchemy* OR *ankr* OR *bsc-dataseed* OR *mainnet* OR *binance* OR *polygon-rpc*)
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest
| ContextImageFileName=/\\pythonw?\.exe$/i
| DomainName=/(rpc|web3|infura|alchemy|ankr|bsc-dataseed|mainnet|binance|polygon-rpc)/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name=pythonw.exe OR All_Traffic.process_name=python.exe) (All_Traffic.dest_host="*rpc*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*web3*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*infura*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*alchemy*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*ankr*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*bsc-dataseed*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*mainnet*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*binance*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where (All_Traffic.process_name=pythonw.exe OR All_Traffic.process_name=python.exe) (All_Traffic.dest_host="*rpc*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*web3*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*infura*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*alchemy*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*ankr*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*bsc-dataseed*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*mainnet*" OR All_Traffic.dest_host="*binance*") by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest All_Traffic.dest_host All_Traffic.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Non-browser process touching Chrome/Edge 'Login Data' and 'Web Data' credential stores AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts ACR Stealer's credential-access step: reading Chrome/Edge Login Data and Web Data SQLite DBs and invoking DPAPI to decrypt saved passwords, cookies, and tokens. Fires when a process other than the browser itself creates/copies/accesses these exact files under the browser User Data path. Rationale: The article's verbatim code blocks name 'Login Data' and 'Web Data' as the exact SQLite DBs ACR reads before DPAPI decryption; a non-browser process touching those files under the browser User Data path is a high-fidelity credential-theft signal. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/intelligence-insights-may-2026/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup or endpoint-DLP agents indexing the user profile
  • Browser sync/migration utilities and password-manager importers
  • Antivirus/EDR file scanners reading the DB (usually excluded above)
  • Enterprise browser-management tooling reading profile data
  • Chrome/Edge helper processes with a renamed image
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("code42service.exe","crashplanservice.exe","backup.exe","1password.exe","keepass.exe","dlpagent.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the accessing process image/path and hash; confirm it is not a sanctioned backup/DLP agent and check its parent chain back to mshta/rundll32/pythonw. 2) Contain: isolate the host and IMMEDIATELY revoke the user's browser session tokens and M365 refresh tokens (passwords rotate is insufficient per Microsoft guidance). 3) Hunt: check for exfil of the copied DB and for OneDrive/SharePoint/PDF collection on the same host; force sign-out of all sessions for the affected identity.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Web Data","Cookies")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data", @"\BraveSoftware\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","explorer.exe","searchindexer.exe","onedrive.exe","msmpeng.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

Endpoint beaconing to ACR Stealer ClickFix campaign payload-host / C2 domains AICommand & Control High
Hunts network connections to the corroborated ACR Stealer campaign infrastructure (payload hosts and C2), including creativecommunityinfo.art, enhanceblabber.cc, sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net and the .icu/.sale rotation set. Straight IOC match for confirmed campaign domains. Rationale: These are the campaign domains cross-confirmed between Microsoft's Campaign 2 table (creativecommunityinfo.art payload host, enhanceblabber.cc C2), Brad Duncan's SANS diary (sphere-api.dialectosphere.in.net), and Red Canary (claude-desktop.gitlab.io) — direct IOC matches with negligible legitimate traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/07/16/acr-stealer-two-observed-intrusion-chains-amid-increased-threat-activity/ • https://isc.sans.edu/diary/33018 • https://redcanary.com/blog/threat-intelligence/intelligence-insights-may-2026/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researchers/sandboxes deliberately resolving the IOCs
  • Threat-intel enrichment tooling pre-resolving domains for scoring
  • DNS sinkhole/telemetry appliances logging blocked lookups as 'queries'
  • Stale browser tabs re-resolving a since-seized domain
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("nslookup.exe","dig.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("svc-threatintel","soc-analyst"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process and whether resolution succeeded/connected; because domains rotate, treat any hit as high-priority and pull the host's full process tree. 2) Contain: block the domains and resolved IPs at proxy/DNS/firewall, isolate the host, and revoke the user's tokens. 3) Hunt: pivot to the resolved IP for co-hosted rotation domains, and sweep for the ClickFix RunMRU / rundll32-WebDAV / pythonw markers on any host that queried these.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (iocs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

ImDnsActivity

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'

falsepositives:

    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high

logsource:
