detection:
    selection_schtasks:
        Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
        CommandLine|contains: '/create'
    selection_payload:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'powershell'
            - 'cmd.exe'
            - 'rundll32'
            - '-enc'
            - 'FromBase64'
            - '\Users\Public'
            - '\AppData\'
    condition: selection_schtasks and selection_payload
falsepositives:
    - GPO-driven scheduled tasks, MDT/SCCM imaging
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name="schtasks.exe" AND Processes.process="*/create*"
      AND (Processes.process="*powershell*" OR Processes.process="*cmd.exe*"
        OR Processes.process="*rundll32*" OR Processes.process="*-enc*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*\Users\Public*"
        OR Processes.process="*\AppData\*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f") or SHA1 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f") or MD5 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f") or SHA1 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f") or MD5 in~ ("70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["70b5ecc110e074dbca92932c0e840ea3492ea0a43c3f215b71392c12b02213b2", "a14c3ecf5eb3d2543358482e43dc765dbf9ee7a4bec7571f5ecb8829ca719692", "47fa746422f1bf6b7712dc6803378e6a995488007193a7441d790f70d204728f"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)

DoNot Team RTF remote-template injection: Word fetching external template AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the DoNot Team (APT-C-35) initial-access step where a malware-laced RTF uses remote template injection to pull a VBA macro from attacker infrastructure, causing WINWORD.EXE to make an outbound HTTP/HTTPS request to a public host on document open. Article-specific to the Bangladesh-military spear-phishing chain that ultimately drops ejtest.dll. Rationale: Word/RTF making its own outbound web request is the observable footprint of remote template injection (T1221) described in the DoNot chain; corroborated by Cyderes Howler write-up detailing geofenced remote-template fetch of the VBA macro. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyderes.com/howler-cell/tracking-donot-apt-c-35-bangladesh-military-intrusion • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1221 T1566.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate documents on a corporate DMS/SharePoint that reference an intranet template store over HTTP
  • Word add-ins or connected services (e.g. Office telemetry, linked images) calling out on open
  • Users opening web-hosted .docx via Protected View that resolves external resources
  • Mail-merge or template-management workflows that legitimately pull remote .dotm files
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("sharepoint.com","office.com","officeapps.live.com") )
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the RemoteUrl/RemoteIP and reputation; open the source document from the mailbox in a sandbox to confirm an external \\template\\ or http reference in document.xml.rels. 2) Contain: block the destination domain/IP at proxy, quarantine the delivering email across mailboxes by sender/subject, isolate the host if a follow-on DLL (ejtest.dll) or shellcode staging is seen. 3) Hunt: pivot on the same host/user for schtasks creating a OneDrive-named task and for rundll32/loader activity referencing ejtest.dll within 24h.

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","wordview.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80,443,8080)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

DoNot Team second-stage loader: ejtest.dll load / invocation AIInstallation High
Hunts execution of the DoNot Team second-stage DLL 'ejtest.dll', a modular implant with follow-on download capability pulled live off active infrastructure by Cyderes. Fires on the named DLL being loaded into any process or referenced on a command line (e.g. rundll32/regsvr32). Rationale: 'ejtest.dll' is a discrete, named second-stage artifact confirmed by Cyderes as pulled live from DoNot infrastructure; a literal filename match is high-fidelity with near-zero legitimate collision. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyderes.com/howler-cell/tracking-donot-apt-c-35-bangladesh-military-intrusion
ATT&CKT1105 T1218.011
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A benign in-house or third-party product genuinely shipping a DLL coincidentally named ejtest.dll (rare)
  • Security researcher/IR analyst detonating the sample in a monitored lab
  • AV/EDR quarantine or scanning tooling referencing the path in its own command line
  • Backup/indexing agents enumerating a captured sample on an analyst workstation
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the ejtest.dll on disk and compare to Cyderes/public IOCs; identify the loading parent process and its origin (Word chain vs manual). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the loader process tree, capture memory before reboot, block the DLL hash across the fleet. 3) Hunt: pivot to the host's outbound HTTPS beacons (AES/C2), OneDrive-telemetry scheduled task, and preceding WINWORD external template fetch to reconstruct the full DoNot chain.
union
( DeviceImageLoadEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName =~ "ejtest.dll"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActorProc=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Path=FolderPath, SHA256, Source="ImageLoad"),
( DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "ejtest.dll"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActorProc=InitiatingProcessFileName, Cmd=ProcessCommandLine, Path=FolderPath, SHA256, Source="Process")
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "ejtest.dll"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine

DoNot Team scheduled-task persistence masquerading as OneDrive telemetry AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the DoNot Team persistence step: a DLL implant registers a scheduled task disguised as OneDrive telemetry. Fires when schtasks.exe creates a task whose name references OneDrive but the creating parent is not a legitimate OneDrive binary. Rationale: The 'OneDrive telemetry' scheduled-task lure is a named DoNot Team tradecraft detail; anchoring on schtasks /create + OneDrive with a non-OneDrive parent isolates the masquerade from genuine OneDrive updater tasks. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cyderes.com/howler-cell/tracking-donot-apt-c-35-bangladesh-military-intrusion
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise deployment tooling (SCCM/Intune) creating OneDrive-related tasks via a management agent parent
  • Admin scripts re-registering OneDrive sync tasks after an image build
  • GPO/logon scripts (cmd/powershell parent) that legitimately provision OneDrive tasks
  • Third-party backup or DLP products scheduling OneDrive-labeled jobs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("Microsoft.OneDrive","OneDriveStandaloneUpdater")
Response runbook
1) Triage: dump the full task XML (schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml) and inspect the Action — legit OneDrive tasks point to OneDrive.exe/OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe; malicious ones invoke rundll32/loader or a Public/AppData path. 2) Contain: delete the rogue task, isolate host, capture the referenced binary. 3) Hunt: correlate to ejtest.dll load, outbound HTTPS beacon, and the delivering RTF on the same host/user.

| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "/create"
| where ProcessCommandLine has "OneDrive"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("onedrive.exe","onedrivesetup.exe","onedrivestandaloneupdater.exe","explorer.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has "/create" and CommandLine has "OneDrive"
| where ParentProcessName !has "OneDrive"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine

GoSerpent QuarksDumpLocalHash local SAM hive credential extraction AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts GoSerpent's local-hash credential-dumping tool QuarksDumpLocalHash, which extracts local account password hashes from the SAM registry hive. Fires on the named tool binary or on reg.exe saving the SAM hive. Distinct from LSASS-access detections (Mimikatz), targeting the SAM path instead. Rationale: QuarksDumpLocalHash is named as GoSerpent's SAM-hive dumper by Kaspersky; matching the tool name plus the canonical 'reg save hklm\sam' technique covers renamed binaries while staying SAM-specific (not a duplicate of LSASS/Mimikatz rules). Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1003.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin exporting SAM/SYSTEM hives during legitimate password-recovery or migration
  • Backup software snapshotting registry hives
  • Forensic/IR tooling collecting SAM as part of triage
  • Pentest/red-team engagements running QuarkspwDump with authorization
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","wbengine.exe","vssvc.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the acting user is not an authorized admin task; check whether SYSTEM hive was also touched (needed to decrypt SAM). 2) Contain: isolate the host, force-reset all local account passwords on that machine, capture the tool binary. 3) Hunt: look for GoSerpent/ThumbcacheService presence, Mimikatz LSASS access, and subsequent authentication to network shares using the dumped local accounts.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName has_any ("QuarksDump","QuarkspwDump")
    or ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName has "QuarksDump"
    or (FileName =~ "reg.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "save" and ProcessCommandLine has @"hklm\sam")

| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("QuarksDump","QuarkspwDump")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "reg.exe" and CommandLine has "save" and CommandLine has @"hklm\sam")

GoSerpent ThumbcacheService collection: password-protected 7-Zip archiving of office documents AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts GoSerpent's ThumbcacheService file-collection behaviour: staging sensitive documents (.doc/.docx/.pdf/.xls/.xlsx) and archiving them with password-protected 7-Zip, often from C:\Users\Public\. Fires on 7-Zip 'add' with a password flag over office-document targets or the Public staging directory. Rationale: Securelist details ThumbcacheService staging collected .doc/.docx/.pdf/.xls/.xlsx into C:\Users\Public\ and archiving with password-protected 7-Zip — the '-p' flag + office-doc/Public targets is the article-specific collection fingerprint. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1560.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User manually creating a password-protected archive of documents to email
  • IT packaging document sets for transfer with 7-Zip and a password
  • Backup/archival jobs compressing user profile documents
  • Legal/e-discovery exports zipping office files with encryption
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("explorer.exe","7zfm.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: locate the output archive and staging DB in C:\Users\Public\; determine whether the parent is a service host (ThumbcacheService) rather than an interactive user. 2) Contain: isolate host, preserve the archive and DB for scoping stolen data, block/remove the ThumbcacheService binary and service. 3) Hunt: pivot to TmcLoader/TmcPayload activity and to writes of the archive to network shares (staging for exfil).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("7z.exe","7za.exe","7zr.exe","7zg.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "-p"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any (".doc",".docx",".pdf",".xls",".xlsx") or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Users\Public\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("7z.exe","7za.exe","7zr.exe","7zg.exe")
| where CommandLine has "-p"
| where CommandLine has_any (".doc",".docx",".pdf",".xls",".xlsx") or CommandLine has @"\Users\Public\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

GoSerpent toolset artifacts: ThumbcacheService / TmcLoader / TmcPayload / Stowaway / McMx drop AIInstallation Medium
Hunting sweep for on-disk artifacts of the GoSerpent toolset named by Kaspersky — the ThumbcacheService DLL/service and the second-wave tools TmcLoader, TmcPayload, Stowaway, and McMx RAT. Fires on file creation or process execution matching these tool names. Broad-net hunt to surface the campaign toolkit on any endpoint. Rationale: These are the exact tool names Kaspersky attributes to the GoSerpent campaign; a filename/service-name sweep is a low-effort, campaign-specific hunt. 'ThumbcacheService' is not a legitimate Windows service, raising confidence for that term. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Generic tool names 'Stowaway'/'McMx' colliding with unrelated open-source binaries a developer downloaded
  • EDR/AV quarantine copies of these samples on analyst hosts
  • IR responders staging captured samples during investigation
  • A benign internal utility coincidentally named with 'Tmc' prefix
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has @"\Quarantine\" and FolderPath !has @"\Windows Defender\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash each hit and compare to Kaspersky/public GoSerpent IOCs; confirm ThumbcacheService is registered as a service and where its DLL lives. 2) Contain: isolate affected hosts, stop/remove the service, block the hashes fleet-wide. 3) Hunt: sweep for the GoSerpent Base64-encoded C2 argument pattern, SOCKS5 listeners, and QuarksDumpLocalHash/Mimikatz credential activity on the same hosts.
union
( DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "ServiceInstalled"
  | where AdditionalFields has "ThumbcacheService" or FileName has "ThumbcacheService"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, Name=FileName, Path=FolderPath, Detail=AdditionalFields, Source="ServiceInstall"),
( DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType == "FileCreated"
  | where FileName has_any ("ThumbcacheService","TmcLoader","TmcPayload","Stowaway","McMx")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, Name=FileName, Path=FolderPath, Detail=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="FileDrop")
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("TmcLoader","TmcPayload","Stowaway","McMx","ThumbcacheService")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine

GoSerpent staged-data exfiltration to network shared drives via TmcPayload/ThumbcacheService AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the GoSerpent exfiltration step where collected/archived data is moved out through network shared drives. Fires when a named collection/exfil tool (TmcLoader, TmcPayload, ThumbcacheService, McMx, Stowaway) writes to a UNC (\\host\share) path — the article's described exfil-via-network-share behaviour. Rationale: Kaspersky states the actor exfiltrates collected data 'through network shared drives' with TmcLoader/TmcPayload after ThumbcacheService collection; anchoring the named tools writing to a UNC path targets that exfil hop specifically rather than generic SMB writes. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/goserpent-backdoor-in-southeast-asia/120687/
ATT&CKT1041 T1039
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate backup/sync agents writing to a file-server share (but not under these tool names)
  • Admin copying archives to a departmental share
  • DFS replication touching UNC paths
  • A benign tool coincidentally named with a 'Tmc'/'Stowaway' string writing to shares
Response runbook
1) Triage: enumerate the destination share and files written; identify whether the source host was recently seen running ThumbcacheService/7-Zip collection. 2) Contain: revoke the writing account's access to the target share, isolate the source host, snapshot the destination share for scoping. 3) Hunt: follow the share to the next hop — which other hosts read the staged archive — and check egress from that host to external C2 to complete the exfil chain.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("TmcLoader","TmcPayload","ThumbcacheService","McMx","Stowaway")
| where FolderPath startswith @"\\"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, ShareName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("TmcLoader","TmcPayload","ThumbcacheService","McMx","Stowaway")
| where TargetFilePath startswith @"\\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003

DeviceEvents

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;

    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)

CISA Adds Exploited SharePoint RCE Zero-Day CVE-2026-58644 to KEV

The Hacker News
2026-07-17 5 use cases 1 technique 6 kill-chain phases detected

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Thursday added a newly patched security flaw impacting Microsoft SharePoint Server to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies to apply the fixes by July 19, 2026. The vulnerability in question is CVE-2026-58644 (CVSS score: 9.8), a critical deserialization

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] SharePoint ToolPane.aspx exploitation POST with forged SignOut Referer (CVE-2026-58644)
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code.

Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.

SharePoint IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell/LOLBin post-RCE (CVE-2026-58644) AIInstallation High
Hunts for command interpreters and discovery LOLBins spawned as children of the SharePoint IIS worker process w3wp.exe. Successful exploitation of the CVE-2026-58644 deserialization RCE executes attacker code inside the w3wp context; a healthy SharePoint farm produces near-zero w3wp child processes, so any cmd/powershell/certutil/whoami/net child is high-signal. Rationale: w3wp.exe is the SharePoint/IIS worker; a legitimate farm virtually never spawns cmd/powershell/certutil children. CISA MAR-251132 and Microsoft's ToolShell reporting confirm this same family drops shells under w3wp — the parent+child pair is the article's RCE impact made concrete. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/14/cisa-urges-sharepoint-hardening-after-new-exploitations • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/07/22/disrupting-active-exploitation-of-on-premises-sharepoint-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar25-218a
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint timer/health analyzer jobs invoking stsadm or PowerShell during patch installation
  • Admins running Get-SPProduct / Config Wizard (psconfig) that shells out from an app-pool context during upgrades
  • Monitoring agents (SCOM/Nagios) that execute discovery commands under IIS identity
  • Legitimate custom web parts that shell out to cmd (rare, should be baselined and allowlisted)
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("psconfig","stsadm -o","SPProductVersionTimerJob") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "OWSTIMER")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Pull the full process tree for the alerting w3wp child — capture ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, and the initiating account. Compare timing to any patch/psconfig maintenance window; genuine exploitation will show ad-hoc discovery (whoami/net) with no change ticket. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the SharePoint host from the network, kill the child process, and snapshot memory. Treat the farm as compromised — do NOT reboot before capturing artifacts. 3) HUNT: Search the same host for newly written .aspx files in LAYOUTS, command lines referencing MachineKey/ValidationKey (see companion UCs), and outbound connections from w3wp. Rotate IIS machine keys AFTER artifact removal per CISA guidance.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","certutil.exe","whoami.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","nltest.exe","bitsadmin.exe","cscript.exe","wscript.exe","mshta.exe","reg.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent

| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any (@"\cmd.exe", @"\powershell.exe", @"\pwsh.exe", @"\certutil.exe", @"\whoami.exe", @"\net.exe", @"\net1.exe", @"\nltest.exe", @"\bitsadmin.exe", @"\cscript.exe", @"\wscript.exe", @"\mshta.exe", @"\reg.exe")
| where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Webshell / DLL dropped in SharePoint LAYOUTS web path (spinstall0.aspx, CVE-2026-58644) AIInstallation High
Detects creation of .aspx/.ashx/.asax/.dll files in SharePoint web-accessible directories (TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS, wss\VirtualDirectories, ISAPI) by w3wp.exe or a shell. Post-RCE the actor writes a webshell — publicly reported as spinstall0.aspx — into LAYOUTS to persist and to exfiltrate the IIS machine keys. Rationale: The SharePoint LAYOUTS/ISAPI/VirtualDirectories paths are web-reachable; a new .aspx there written by w3wp is the textbook ToolShell webshell drop. Filename spinstall0.aspx and these directories are corroborated in CISA MAR-251132 and Microsoft's ToolShell blog for this exact machine-key-theft chain. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar25-218a • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2025/07/22/disrupting-active-exploitation-of-on-premises-sharepoint-vulnerabilities/ • https://www.trellix.com/blogs/research/toolshell-unleashed-decoding-the-sharepoint-attack-chain/
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint cumulative update / psconfig deploying new solution (.wsp) files that stage .aspx and .dll into LAYOUTS
  • Third-party SharePoint add-in installation (msiexec/SPSolution deploy) writing signed DLLs
  • Developer publishing a custom web part to a farm during a change window
  • Antivirus quarantine-and-restore cycling files in web directories
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","psconfig.exe") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("SolutionDeployment","install-spsolution",".wsp"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Retrieve the dropped file's SHA256 and contents; a genuine webshell will reference Request/Response, eval, or MachineKey/ValidationKey extraction. Confirm the writer was w3wp.exe with no matching solution-deploy change ticket. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, preserve the file (copy, don't delete), and block the source IP at the perimeter. Per CISA, remove intrusion artifacts BEFORE rotating machine keys. 3) HUNT: Grep IIS logs for GET/POST to the dropped filename to find operator IPs, pivot to any process reading web.config machine keys, and enumerate all farm servers for the same filename — the webshell is often deployed farm-wide.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Web Server Extensions\15\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", @"\Web Server Extensions\16\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", @"\inetpub\wwwroot\wss\VirtualDirectories", @"\Web Server Extensions\15\ISAPI", @"\Web Server Extensions\16\ISAPI")
| where (FileName endswith ".aspx" or FileName endswith ".ashx" or FileName endswith ".asax" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName startswith "spinstall")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("w3wp.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\TEMPLATE\LAYOUTS", @"\wss\VirtualDirectories", @"\TEMPLATE\ISAPI")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("aspx","ashx","asax","dll") or TargetFileName startswith "spinstall"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("w3wp.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

IIS MachineKey / ValidationKey theft under w3wp lineage (CVE-2026-58644 post-exploit) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects processes descending from the SharePoint worker w3wp.exe whose command line references IIS cryptographic secrets (MachineKey, ValidationKey, DecryptionKey, Get-SPMachineKey). CISA explicitly calls out stealing IIS machine keys as the CVE-2026-58644 post-exploitation objective, enabling forged-ViewState persistent access even after patching. Rationale: CISA names 'stealing IIS machine keys' as the specific CVE-2026-58644 post-exploitation goal; ValidationKey/DecryptionKey/MachineKey are the exact strings the spinstall0.aspx shell extracts. Anchoring the keyword match to w3wp lineage separates attacker harvesting from routine admin key rotation. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/07/14/cisa-urges-sharepoint-hardening-after-new-exploitations • https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/sharepoint-toolshell-zero-day-exploited-in-the-wild-targets-enterprise-servers/
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1555
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • SharePoint admin manually rotating machine keys via Update-SPMachineKey / Set-SPMachineKey after the CISA advisory
  • Farm build automation that sets a consistent machineKey across web front-ends
  • Security team running validation scripts to inventory machine keys during IR
  • Config-management tooling (DSC/Ansible) templating web.config machineKey sections
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName in~ ("sp_farm","svc-spadmin") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Set-SPMachineKey","Update-SPMachineKey"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the invoking account is a known SharePoint farm admin and whether an approved key-rotation/IR task explains it. Attacker activity is spawned from w3wp with no interactive admin session. 2) CONTAIN: If unexplained, treat the machine keys as compromised — isolate the host, and plan a coordinated ValidationKey/DecryptionKey rotation across ALL farm servers (after removing webshells, per CISA order of operations). 3) HUNT: Correlate with UC2 (webshell drop) and IIS logs for forged-ViewState POSTs; forged machine keys grant persistent access indistinguishable from legit traffic, so review authentication anomalies going forward.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe" or InitiatingProcessParentFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","MachineKey","Get-SPMachineKey","MachineKeySection","System.Web.Configuration.MachineKeySection")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\w3wp.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("ValidationKey","DecryptionKey","MachineKey","Get-SPMachineKey","MachineKeySection")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

SharePoint ToolPane.aspx exploitation POST with forged SignOut Referer (CVE-2026-58644) AIDelivery Medium
Detects the network-facing exploitation signature of the CVE-2026-58644 chain in IIS access logs: an unauthenticated POST to /_layouts/*/ToolPane.aspx carrying a forged Referer of /_layouts/SignOut.aspx used to bypass authentication before the deserialization RCE. This targets the initial_access step directly on the wire. Rationale: The POST-to-ToolPane.aspx with a Referer forged to /_layouts/SignOut.aspx is the documented ToolShell auth-bypass signature CISA/Microsoft tie to this exact SharePoint machine-key-theft chain; it is a pre-auth network artifact with essentially no benign equivalent. Defender/Datadog/Falcon left empty as IIS URI+Referer telemetry is not in those data sets in this tenant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/analysis-reports/ar25-218a • https://www.anomali.com/blog/detecting-the-toolshell-sharepoint-exploit • https://www.forescout.com/blog/threat-analysis-microsoft-sharepoint-toolshell-exploits/
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate SharePoint page authoring that genuinely POSTs to ToolPane.aspx (Referer will NOT be SignOut.aspx, so the combined condition largely excludes this)
  • Vulnerability scanners (Tenable/Qualys) replaying the ToolShell PoC during authorized testing
  • Security team validation of the patch using the public exploit
  • Load balancer / reverse proxy rewriting Referer headers in a way that coincidentally matches (rare)
Suppression filter
| where cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8") and csUserAgent !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Tenable")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Record the source cIP, User-Agent, and scStatus. A 200/302 on this request indicates likely successful bypass; correlate the same cIP for follow-on GETs to newly created .aspx files. 2) CONTAIN: Block the source IP at the WAF/perimeter and, if a 2xx was returned, isolate the SharePoint server and treat the farm as compromised. 3) HUNT: Pivot on the source IP across all farm front-ends, then jump to UC1/UC2/UC3 to confirm w3wp child processes, webshell drops, and machine-key theft on the targeted host. Verify AMSI integration is enabled per CISA hardening.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has "/ToolPane.aspx"
| where csReferer has "/_layouts/SignOut.aspx"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csReferer, scStatus, csUserAgent, csUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-07-16 12 use cases 12 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

From late April 2026 to mid-June 2026, Microsoft Defender Experts observed increased ACR Stealer activity across customer environments. These campaigns are successfully using ClickFix lures to steal browser credentials, authentication tokens, and sensitive documents from enterprise environments. The post ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ACR Stealer: Two observed intrusion chains amid increased threat activity
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.

| where Timestamp > ago(1d)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Exposed Pheditor admin editor (pheditor.php) reachable over HTTP AIDelivery Medium
Surfaces any web request to pheditor.php, the single-file admin editor that ships with the hardcoded default password 'admin' (CVE-2026-55579). Because there is no forced password change, any internet-reachable pheditor.php is effectively an unauthenticated RCE endpoint, so simply locating exposed instances is the highest-leverage first pivot. Rationale: Keys on the literal endpoint path pheditor.php confirmed in the advisory and in the live repo source. Defender AH has no web-access-log table so defender_kql is empty; on Apache/nginx front ends substitute CommonSecurityLog.RequestURL for W3CIISLog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php • https://osv.dev/list
ATT&CKT1190 T1595.002
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer/sysadmin using Pheditor as an intended file editor
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Nuclei) probing for pheditor.php
  • Uptime/monitoring checks hitting the admin path
  • Search-engine or asset-inventory crawlers indexing the web root
Suppression filter
| where cIP !startswith "10." and cIP !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the host actually serves pheditor.php and whether it is internet-reachable; check the source IPs and user-agents hitting it for scanner vs. human patterns. Step 2 (contain): If exposed to untrusted networks, block the path at the WAF/reverse proxy, take the editor offline, and change the admin password off the default. Step 3 (hunt): Review UC for POST volume (spray), action=terminal requests, php spawning shells, and newly-written .php files on the same host to establish whether default creds were already used.
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/pheditor.php"
| summarize Requests=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Methods=make_set(csMethod), Statuses=make_set(scStatus), UAs=make_set(csUserAgent) by cIP, sSiteName
| order by Requests desc

description: Detects web requests to pheditor.php, the single-file PHP admin editor shipping with the hardcoded default password 'admin' (CVE-2026-55579).

logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection:
    cs-uri-stem|endswith: '/pheditor.php'
  condition: selection
level: medium
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*pheditor.php*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status, Web.http_method
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*pheditor.php*" by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.http_user_agent, Web.status, Web.http_method
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
