Repeated authentication POSTs to Pheditor (default-credential guessing / spray) AIDelivery Medium
Detects a source IP sending many POST requests to pheditor.php in a short window — the shape of default-credential guessing against an instance that ships with password 'admin' and enforces no lockout, expiry, or forced change (CVE-2026-55579). Note: Pheditor returns HTTP 200 for BOTH success and failure, so this pivots on request volume rather than status code. Rationale: Because the app returns 200 on both correct and incorrect passwords (body 'The entry password is not correct.' on failure), a status-code 401->200 rule cannot work here; volume of POSTs to the single login endpoint is the reliable brute/spray signal. Threshold is commented and tunable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1110.001 T1078.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An admin repeatedly re-saving files (each POST hits pheditor.php)
  • Automated CI/CD or backup script interacting with the editor
  • A misconfigured session causing repeated re-login prompts
  • Load-balancer health checks POSTing to the app root
Suppression filter
| search NOT src IN ("127.0.0.1","::1")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the offending source IP's full request sequence; distinguish an admin doing many file saves (varied actions) from monotonic login attempts (repeated pheditor_password submissions). Step 2 (contain): Block the source IP at the WAF, force the admin password off 'admin', and invalidate active sessions. Step 3 (hunt): If any request in the burst was followed by action=terminal or upload-file activity, treat as compromise and pivot to endpoint UCs (php spawning shell / webshell writes).
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| where csUriStem =~ "/pheditor.php" and csMethod == "POST"
| summarize Attempts=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), UAs=make_set(csUserAgent) by cIP, sSiteName
| where Attempts >= 10   // 10 = single-user admin editor should see one login POST per session; 10 POSTs/hr from one IP is abnormal
| order by Attempts desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*pheditor.php*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count >= 10
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*pheditor.php*" Web.http_method=POST by Web.src, Web.dest, _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count >= 10
| sort - count
Pheditor terminal RCE invocation via HTTP (action=terminal / command=) AIExploitation High
Detects HTTP requests to pheditor.php carrying the terminal action and command parameter — the built-in terminal feature that yields immediate RCE once the default 'admin' password is used (CVE-2026-55579, and the related command-sanitization bypass CVE-2026-55578). Requires a WAF/proxy that logs query string and/or request body. Rationale: action=terminal and the command parameter are the exact terminal-feature strings confirmed from the Pheditor source. These params are POST body so detection requires WAF/proxy body or query logging; pair with the endpoint UC (php spawning shell) for confirmation where body capture is unavailable. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1190 T1059.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin using the Pheditor terminal for routine server tasks
  • Internal automation invoking the terminal action
  • Security testers validating the CVE in a sanctioned pentest
  • WAF false-parsing another app's 'command=' parameter (scope by pheditor.php path mitigates)
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("127.0.0.1","::1")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the decoded command string from RequestContext/body and the source IP; determine if the caller is a known admin from an expected network. Step 2 (contain): If unrecognized, isolate the web host, kill live php/shell child processes, block the source IP, and rotate the admin password off default. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to endpoint telemetry for php->sh/bash execution and any newly-dropped .php files; review outbound connections from the web-server user for C2 or data staging.
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where RequestURL has "pheditor.php"
| where RequestURL has "action=terminal" or RequestContext has "action=terminal" or RequestURL has "command=" or RequestContext has "command="
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestContext, RequestClientApplication
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web-server/PHP process spawning a shell (Pheditor terminal RCE on host) AIExploitation High
Highest-fidelity confirmation of Pheditor terminal RCE: a PHP interpreter or web-server process (php, php-fpm, php-cgi, apache2/httpd, w3wp) spawning an interactive shell or recon binary under the web-server account. This is the on-host footprint of the action=terminal command execution described in CVE-2026-55579 / CVE-2026-55578. Rationale: A file-editor's web process spawning /bin/sh + recon commands under www-data/apache is the deterministic on-host signature of the pheditor terminal feature; parent set covers php-fpm, mod_php (apache2/httpd) and IIS FastCGI (php-cgi.exe under w3wp). Datadog covers the Windows FastCGI case; Linux auditd lacks a clean parent field. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1059.004 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A PHP application legitimately shelling out (image thumbnailing via ImageMagick, git hooks, cron wrappers)
  • Deployment scripts run as the web-server user
  • Monitoring agents executing whoami/uname under the app account
  • Composer/artisan style tooling invoked by php-fpm
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("convert","gs ","ffmpeg","git ","composer"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the child process command line and full process tree; benign PHP shell-outs are narrow (e.g. convert, git), whereas RCE shows id/whoami/curl or an interactive shell. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, suspend the php-fpm/apache worker, capture volatile memory, and block any C2 IPs seen from the web account. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate .php/.phtml files written by the web process (webshell drop), review pheditor.php modification time, and correlate with inbound action=terminal requests in web/WAF logs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(php|php-fpm|php-cgi)([0-9.]+)?(\.exe)?$" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("sh","bash","dash","zsh","id","whoami","uname","curl","wget","nc","ncat","python","python3","perl")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Web-server/PHP process writing new PHP webshell to web root AIInstallation Medium
Detects a PHP/web-server process creating a new .php/.phtml/.phar file — the on-host result of abusing Pheditor's file-upload (action=upload-file) or file-write editor features to drop a webshell after authenticating with the default password (CVE-2026-55579). Excludes pheditor.php itself (covered separately). Rationale: Pheditor's upload-file action and file editor let an authenticated (default-cred) attacker write arbitrary files; a web process creating new executable PHP content in the web root is the classic webshell-drop signature. Self-file pheditor.php excluded to route those to the dedicated modification UC. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate deployments/CMS updates writing PHP cache or compiled templates (Twig/Blade cache) under the web user
  • Composer installing PHP packages into the web root
  • A developer legitimately using Pheditor to create new PHP files
  • Plugin/theme installers extracting .php archives
Suppression filter
| where FolderPath !has "cache" and FolderPath !has "vendor" and FolderPath !has "storage/framework"
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Open the newly-written file — template/cache artifacts are auto-generated and predictable, whereas a webshell contains eval/system/base64_decode/assert or request-parameter passthrough. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file, isolate the host, and rotate the Pheditor admin password off default. Step 3 (hunt): Search web/WAF logs for subsequent GET/POST requests to the new file path, and check for php spawning shells and outbound C2 from the web account.

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName matches regex @"(?i)^(php|php-fpm|php-cgi)([0-9.]+)?(\.exe)?$" or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("httpd","apache2","w3wp.exe")
| where FileName endswith ".php" or FileName endswith ".phtml" or FileName endswith ".phar" or FileName endswith ".php5"
| where FileName !~ "pheditor.php"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc

| where TargetFileName !endswith "pheditor.php"

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Modification of Pheditor source file (pheditor.php) — hardcoded hash tamper AIInstallation Medium
Monitors writes/renames to pheditor.php itself. The advisory notes the SHA-512 default-password hash is stored at pheditor.php:11 and the in-app password change rewrites the hash directly into the source file — so any modification is either a legitimate credential change, a hardening action, or attacker persistence editing the admin hash. Flags changes lacking a change-control ticket. Rationale: The advisory explicitly states the SHA-512 hash lives at pheditor.php:11 and the password-change feature writes the new hash back into the source file; FIM on this exact filename catches both legitimate hardening (default hash replaced) and malicious hash swaps for persistent admin access. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-p4h7-p9rj-2pq2 • https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pheditor/pheditor/main/pheditor.php
ATT&CKT1554 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate admin changing the Pheditor password via the app (rewrites the hash by design)
  • Scheduled deployment/git pull updating the file to a patched version (2.0.6+)
  • Sysadmin manually editing the file to remove the default hash (hardening)
  • Backup/restore operations touching the web root
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("php","php-fpm","php-cgi","httpd","apache2")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the initiating process and user — an in-app change is written by php-fpm/apache, whereas an editor (vim/nano/notepad) or unexpected account is worth scrutiny; confirm against change-control records. Step 2 (contain): If unsanctioned, capture the pre-change hash from backups, restore a known-good pheditor.php, and force a fresh non-default password. Step 3 (hunt): Diff the modified file for an injected/attacker-controlled hash or added PHP, and correlate with prior action=terminal / webshell activity on the host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pheditor.php"
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, PreviousFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "pheditor.php"
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, EventType, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EnvoyExtensionPolicy Lua with double-slash path traversal to secrets (CVE-2026-53713) AIExploitation High
Hunts EnvoyExtensionPolicy create/update whose inline Lua contains the exact double-slash bypass paths (//etc/passwd, //var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, //proc/self/environ, //certs/) that defeat the is_critical_path check in security.lua. This is the concrete exploit signature for arbitrary file read from the Envoy Gateway controller pod during Strict validation. Rationale: Uses the exact double-slash payload paths named in the advisory (//etc/passwd, //var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token, //proc/self/environ, //certs/) scoped to the envoyextensionpolicies resource — legitimate Lua policies never reference these. Cross-checked GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f and the related GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/golang/github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/CVE-2026-22771/
ATT&CKT1190 T1212 T1083
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security team submitting a sanctioned validation/PoC policy to confirm patch status
  • Automated CVE-scanner or admission-controller test harness replaying the exploit manifest
  • A Lua policy that legitimately references /certs/ (single slash) mis-typed with a double slash by an operator
  • Backup/GitOps replay re-applying an old exploit manifest already stored in the repo
Suppression filter
| where SubmitUser !in ("system:serviceaccount:security-tools:cve-scanner") and UserAgent !has "validation-harness"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full requestObject for the flagged EnvoyExtensionPolicy and identify the submitting user/SA, source IP and userAgent; confirm the Lua references the double-slash sensitive paths. 2) Contain: delete the policy, rotate the envoy-gateway controller ServiceAccount token and any TLS keys reachable from the controller pod, and revoke the submitter's RBAC to create EnvoyExtensionPolicy. 3) Hunt: check the resource status/response for leaked token or file contents (see companion UC), and review kube audit for the envoy-gateway SA being used from unexpected sources afterward.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("//etc/passwd","//var/run/secrets","//proc/self/environ","//certs/")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), SrcIPs = tostring(User.extra)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, UserAgent, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CLOUD
index=* sourcetype="kube:apiserver:audit" "objectRef.resource"="envoyextensionpolicies" (verb="create" OR verb="update" OR verb="patch")

Leaked SA token / file contents in EnvoyExtensionPolicy status (CVE-2026-53713 disclosure) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the actual secret disclosure: an envoyextensionpolicies audit record whose responseObject/status contains a JWT (service-account token), /etc/passwd content, or a PEM private key returned by the failed Strict validation. This confirms exploitation succeeded rather than just being attempted. Rationale: The related advisory confirms the SA token is 'returned in an error which will be displayed in the resource status'; eyJhbGciOi is the constant base64 prefix of a JWT header and root:x:0:0 is the invariant first line of /etc/passwd — both are high-fidelity content markers requiring RequestResponse-level audit. Cross-checked GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22
ATT&CKT1528 T1552.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A policy legitimately referencing a JWT sample string in a comment (rare)
  • Audit policy not set to RequestResponse level so responseObject is empty (false negative, not FP)
  • Security testing that intentionally reproduces the disclosure in a lab cluster
  • A PEM string embedded in an unrelated but co-located config field captured in the same response
Response runbook
1) Triage: extract the leaked material from responseObject — decode the JWT to identify which ServiceAccount was disclosed and its namespace/audience. 2) Contain: immediately rotate/delete that ServiceAccount token (delete the SA's token secret / bounce the pod to force projection refresh) and rotate any disclosed TLS private keys; treat the token as compromised. 3) Hunt: search kube audit for that SA's token being replayed (new sourceIPs, verbs it does not normally perform) and pivot to the companion token-reuse UC.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend RespStr = tostring(ResponseObject), StatusStr = tostring(ResponseStatus)
| where RespStr has_any ("eyJhbGciOi","root:x:0:0","BEGIN RSA PRIVATE KEY","BEGIN PRIVATE KEY","serviceaccount/token") or StatusStr has_any ("eyJhbGciOi","root:x:0:0")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, ResponseStatus, RespStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

EnvoyExtensionPolicy Lua invoking os/io/debug file primitives AIExploitation Medium
Broader hunt for EnvoyExtensionPolicy manifests whose inline Lua calls filesystem/OS primitives (io.open, io.popen, os.getenv, os.execute, os.remove, debug.getinfo) — the building blocks any variant of this exploit needs to read the controller pod's files, catching payloads that use paths other than the four named in the advisory. Rationale: Reading a file from Lua requires io/os primitives; legitimate Envoy request-processing Lua manipulates headers/bodies and rarely touches io.open/os.execute, so their presence in a submitted policy is a strong pre-execution signal even when the payload uses a novel path. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://github.com/envoyproxy/gateway/security/advisories/GHSA-xrwg-mqj6-6m22
ATT&CKT1059 T1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate advanced Lua filter that reads a mounted config file via io.open
  • os.getenv used to read a benign env var for routing logic
  • Developer testing a Lua snippet copied from a tutorial that includes os.time/os.date near os.execute
  • Vendor-provided policy template that legitimately uses debug for logging
Response runbook
1) Triage: read the full Lua body from requestObject and determine whether the io/os call targets sensitive paths or is benign routing logic. 2) Contain: if malicious, delete the policy and rotate controller credentials; if the cluster runs a vulnerable version, prioritise upgrade to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1. 3) Hunt: pivot to the double-slash and status-disclosure UCs for the same policy name and submitter.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend ReqStr = tostring(RequestObject)
| where ReqStr has_any ("io.open","io.popen","os.getenv","os.execute","os.remove","debug.getinfo")
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubmitUser, Verb, RequestUri, UserAgent, ReqStr
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Anomalous EnvoyExtensionPolicy submitter / suspicious policy name AIDelivery Medium
Profiles who creates EnvoyExtensionPolicy resources to surface rare submitters, and flags policy names containing exploit markers (poc, test, bypass, exploit, passwd). Because the exploit requires an attacker to create/patch the policy via the K8s API, unusual submitters are a leading indicator. Rationale: EnvoyExtensionPolicy objects are normally authored by a small, stable set of platform/GitOps identities; the summarize-by-submitter surfaces rare creators without a hard-coded allowlist, and the name markers catch dropped PoC manifests. Grouping/rarity is evaluated at rule level for Datadog. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f
ATT&CKT1190 T1078
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate GitOps controller (ArgoCD/Flux SA) creating policies — high count, benign
  • A developer genuinely naming a policy 'canary-test' or 'lua-test'
  • First-time onboarding of a new platform engineer who legitimately creates a policy
  • CI pipeline SA applying policies from a new namespace
Suppression filter
| where SubmitUser !startswith "system:serviceaccount:argocd:" and SubmitUser !startswith "system:serviceaccount:flux-system:"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for any rare submitter or exploit-marker name, retrieve the policy body and check for Lua io/os calls or double-slash paths. 2) Contain: if the submitter is unexpected, revoke their create/patch RBAC on envoyextensionpolicies and delete the policy. 3) Hunt: correlate the submitter identity across other CRDs and namespaces for further unauthorized changes.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Verb in ("create","update","patch")
| where RequestUri has "envoyextensionpolicies"
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), PolicyName = tostring(ObjectRef.name)
| extend SuspiciousName = PolicyName has_any ("poc","test","bypass","exploit","passwd")
| summarize Count=count(), Policies=make_set(PolicyName, 25), AnySuspicious=max(tolong(SuspiciousName)), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by SubmitUser, UserAgent
| order by Count asc

Vulnerable Envoy Gateway version exposed to CVE-2026-53713 AIReconnaissance Medium
Inventory hunt that flags hosts/images running an Envoy Gateway version affected by CVE-2026-53713 (>=1.8.0-rc.0 <1.8.1, or <1.7.4) so the exploitable surface is remediated to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1 before an attacker submits a malicious EnvoyExtensionPolicy. Rationale: Uses the exact CVE id and the affected/fixed version ranges from the advisory (fixed >=1.7.4 and >=1.8.1). This is the only pivot expressible on Defender/Sentinel native telemetry since the attack itself lives in K8s audit logs; relies on container/software vuln assessment picking up the envoyproxy/gateway package. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f
ATT&CKT1190
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A patched version mis-fingerprinted by TVM as vulnerable (stale scan)
  • An image tag pinned to a fixed digest but labelled with an old version string
  • Non-production/lab Envoy Gateway flagged alongside prod
  • TVM not yet ingesting the CVE definition (false negative, not FP)
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the reported SoftwareVersion is genuinely <1.7.4 or in 1.8.0-rc.0..1.8.1 and that the instance accepts EnvoyExtensionPolicy submissions. 2) Contain: restrict RBAC so only trusted identities can create/patch EnvoyExtensionPolicy, and apply the Lua-docs Warning-section workarounds until patched. 3) Hunt: upgrade to >=1.7.4 / >=1.8.1 and retro-scan kube audit for prior exploit attempts against the affected cluster.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53713"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by Timestamp desc
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId == "CVE-2026-53713"
| project TimeGenerated, DeviceName, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by TimeGenerated desc
Envoy Gateway ServiceAccount token reuse for anomalous K8s API actions AIActions on Objectives Medium
Post-exploitation hunt: the envoy-gateway controller ServiceAccount (system:serviceaccount:envoy-gateway-system:envoy-gateway) performing actions it never legitimately performs — creating/deleting pods, exec/attach into pods, reading kube-system secrets, or touching cluster RBAC — which indicates the disclosed token is being replayed against the API server. Rationale: The advisory states the disclosed token can be used to 'read sensitive information from the K8s API Server'; the envoy-gateway controller SA legitimately manages EnvoyProxy infra in its own namespace but never execs into pods, reads kube-system secrets, or edits cluster RBAC — so those verbs under that identity are strong reuse signals. SA name/namespace confirmed from Envoy Gateway deployment docs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wcrf-9vrr-854f • https://gateway.envoyproxy.io/docs/tasks/operations/deployment-mode/
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1552.001
Data sources
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Envoy Gateway upgrade/migration job temporarily granting the SA broader RBAC
  • A future controller version that legitimately reads a secret in a shared namespace
  • Cluster admin impersonating the SA for troubleshooting (kubectl --as)
  • Backup tooling running under the same SA reading secrets broadly
Suppression filter
| where UserAgent !startswith "envoy-gateway/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: for each hit compare sourceIPs and userAgent against the controller pod's normal client (in-cluster pod IP, controller userAgent); an external IP or kubectl/curl userAgent is high-confidence token theft. 2) Contain: rotate the envoy-gateway SA token immediately, cordon/quarantine any pods created by the SA, and review/revert RBAC changes. 3) Hunt: enumerate every action taken by the token since the disclosure event and check for new workloads, exfil connections, or additional credential reads.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| extend SubmitUser = tostring(User.username), Resource = tostring(ObjectRef.resource), NS = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace)
| where SubmitUser == "system:serviceaccount:envoy-gateway-system:envoy-gateway"
| where (Verb in ("create","delete") and Resource in ("pods","pods/exec","pods/attach"))
     or (Resource == "secrets" and NS == "kube-system")
     or (Resource in ("clusterrolebindings","rolebindings","clusterroles"))
| project TimeGenerated, SubmitUser, Verb, Resource, NS, ObjName=tostring(ObjectRef.name), UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc

ThreatsDay: Game Cheat Spyware, 24-Hour Ransomware, Chrome Sync Stalking + 12 More Stories

The Hacker NewsCisco Talos
2026-07-16 21 use cases 13 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A lot of this week’s trouble starts with something that looks close enough. A familiar repo. A useful installer. A harmless sync setting. Then the handoff goes bad, the box starts talking to someone else, and the damage moves faster than the explanation. Old bugs are back, weak defaults are earning their keep, and some attack paths are so plain they barely feel like research. Here’s the mess.

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Spirals ransomware precursor: IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell from ASP.NET web shell · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — ThreatsDay: Game Cheat Spyware, 24-Hour Ransomware, Chrome Sync Stalking + 12 Mo
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Game-cheat NuGet downloader fetches pepesoft.exe from pepegit666 GitHub/Hugging Face infra · Suspicious browser extension installation · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Starland RAT uses curl.exe to spawn PowerShell stager (WLDR agent decrypt/run) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Spirals ransomware bulk file-encryption burst (single process, high write/rename volume) · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft)
Game-cheat NuGet downloader fetches pepesoft.exe from pepegit666 GitHub/Hugging Face infra AIInstallation High
Hunts the second-stage payload of the 11 malicious NuGet 'game cheat' packages: a .NET DotnetTool downloader that pulls and runs pepesoft.exe from GitHub Releases and Hugging Face paths under the actor username 'pepegit666'. Article-specific because it anchors on the concrete payload filename, the operator handle, and the two hosting services rather than generic .NET tooling. Rationale: Anchors on the exact payload filename pepesoft.exe and the operator handle pepegit666 plus the two named hosting services (GitHub Releases, Hugging Face) from the article — all confirmed by Socket's write-up, so hits are near-certain true positives. Cross-checked against: • https://socket.dev/blog/11-malicious-nuget-tools-pose-as-game-cheats • https://gbhackers.com/11-malicious-nuget-game-cheat-packages/ • https://cyberpress.org/nuget-packages-deploy-spyware/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1105 T1071.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security researcher detonating the pepesoft.exe sample in a sandbox VM
  • Malware-analysis or threat-intel tooling caching the sample under a pepegit666-referencing path
  • Blue-team purple-team exercise replaying the NuGet supply-chain sample
  • EDR quarantine copies retaining the original FileOriginUrl string
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("SANDBOX","MALWARELAB","ANALYSIS"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the SHA256 of pepesoft.exe against VT/Socket; check whether a NuGet DotnetTool (dotnet.exe/.NET tool) was the parent that spawned or wrote it, and pull the FileOriginUrl to confirm the pepegit666 source. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill pepesoft.exe, and block the resolved GitHub/Hugging Face download IPs plus api.telegram.org egress. Step 3 (hunt): Enumerate all NuGet/dotnet tool installs on the host, sweep the org for the 11 package names and any dns.google DoH lookups immediately preceding github raw content connections (the campaign's DoH evasion).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "pepesoft.exe"
   or FileOriginUrl has_any ("pepegit666","huggingface.co","github.com/pepegit666")
   or FileOriginReferrerUrl has "pepegit666"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "pepesoft.exe" or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pepegit666","pepesoft.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Starland RAT uses curl.exe to spawn PowerShell stager (WLDR agent decrypt/run) AICommand & Control High
Detects UAT-11795's distinctive execution hand-off where the Python-based Starland RAT invokes curl.exe which in turn launches a PowerShell stager that decrypts and runs the in-memory WLDR C2 agent. curl.exe as the direct parent of PowerShell is rare and article-specific to this Russian-speaking financially-motivated campaign. Rationale: curl.exe directly spawning PowerShell is the article's named execution primitive for Starland RAT delivering WLDR — an uncommon parent/child pair confirmed by Cisco Talos, giving a low-FP, high-confidence pivot without relying on encoded-PowerShell heuristics. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.talosintelligence.com/uat-11795-deploys-novel-starland-rat-and-bespoke-wldr-c2-implant-in-financially-motivated-campaign/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/russian-hackers-trojanize-webex-zoom-apps-to-push-starland-malware/
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1105 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer or CI script piping a downloaded PowerShell installer via curl (e.g. 'curl ... | powershell')
  • DevOps bootstrap tooling using curl to fetch and run a PS setup script
  • Chocolatey/winget-style install wrappers that call curl then PowerShell
  • Admin one-liners chaining curl and powershell for remote script retrieval
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("chocolatey","choco","winget","\\CI\\","azure-pipelines"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Capture both command lines — confirm whether the PowerShell child references a local encrypted blob/decrypt routine (WLDR stager) versus a benign remote installer URL, and check the grandparent for a trojanized installer name (MobaXterm, WebEx, Zoom, DBeaver, FaceIT). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host and terminate the PowerShell process tree; snapshot memory to recover the in-memory WLDR agent before reboot. Step 3 (hunt): Look for encrypted C2 beaconing from powershell.exe, Remcos/CastleStealer artifacts, browser-credential and crypto-wallet access, and other hosts that ran the same trojanized installer hashes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\curl.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where not(SubjectUserName endswith "$")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Spirals ransomware precursor: IIS worker (w3wp.exe) spawning shell from ASP.NET web shell AIExploitation High
Detects the initial-access step of the Spirals ransomware intrusion: an internet-facing IIS server whose w3wp.exe worker process spawns command/PowerShell/recon binaries, the behavioural signature of the ASP.NET web shell the actor uploaded before establishing persistence and deploying ransomware within 24 hours. Rationale: The article states initial access was an ASP.NET web shell on an internet-facing IIS server; w3wp.exe spawning shells/recon is the direct host-side signature of that web shell and is anomalous on production IIS, giving a low-FP precursor to the sub-24h ransomware deployment. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-game-cheat-spyware-24-hour.html
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1190 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A web app legitimately shelling out (e.g. a management portal running net user/whoami for diagnostics)
  • IIS-hosted monitoring/health-check scripts invoking cmd or PowerShell
  • Deployment tooling running under the app pool identity during a release
  • Admin troubleshooting an app pool via an interactive process under w3wp
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("healthcheck","\\Deploy\\","appcmd list","telemetry"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Review the child command line and the IIS site/app-pool identity; pull recent DeviceFileEvents for newly-created .aspx/.asmx/.ashx files in the web root to locate the dropped web shell. Step 2 (contain): Take the IIS server offline or block inbound to the affected site, preserve the web shell file and IIS logs, and reset the app-pool and any credentials it can reach. Step 3 (hunt): Given the 24h ransomware timeline, immediately hunt for SAM hive dumps, endpoint-security uninstall events, PsExec staging, and mass file-encryption across hosts the server can reach.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "w3wp.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","reg.exe","nltest.exe","systeminfo.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\w3wp.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\cmd.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\net.exe","\\net1.exe","\\whoami.exe","\\reg.exe","\\nltest.exe","\\systeminfo.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: IIS Worker w3wp.exe Spawning Shell or Recon Binary (Spirals Ransomware Web Shell)
id: c8a2f5d9-4b17-4e6c-9a03-1f7d6b2e8c40
description: Detects w3wp.exe spawning command-shell, PowerShell or reconnaissance binaries, indicative of an ASP.NET web shell such as the one used to gain initial access in the Spirals ransomware intrusion.

Spirals ransomware bulk file-encryption burst (single process, high write/rename volume) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Behavioural impact detection for the Spirals Rust-based ransomware that encrypted the victim network within 24 hours: a single non-system process modifying/renaming/deleting thousands of files across many folders in a short window. Grounded in the article's explicit rapid network-wide encryption and same-day payload push. Rationale: Uses the article's explicit fact that Spirals pushed the payload network-wide and encrypted within 24 hours; since no ransom-note name or extension was published, the detection stays behavioural (per-process file-op burst) rather than inventing IOC strings. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/threatsday-game-cheat-spyware-24-hour.html
ATT&CKT1486 T1490 T1489
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veeam/Commvault/backup agents performing large-scale snapshot or restore file operations
  • Disk-encryption rollout (BitLocker/third-party) touching many files at once
  • Bulk media transcoding, video rendering, or large software-build/CI artifact generation
  • Antivirus full-scan quarantining/renaming many files
  • Search-indexer or migration tooling rewriting large directory trees
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("veeam.backup.shell.exe","commvault.exe","cvd.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","BackupAgent.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Inspect the offending process image/path and a sample of touched files — check for new/changed file extensions or a ransom note dropped in the same folders; confirm the process isn't a known backup/encryption agent. Step 2 (contain): Network-isolate the host immediately, kill the process, and disable the account/PsExec path used to push it; preserve one encrypted sample and the note for keying. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for the same binary hash across the fleet (PsExec-style fan-out), check for SAM dumps, endpoint-security uninstalls, VSS/shadow-copy deletion, and Tor connectivity referenced in the ransom workflow.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where ActionType in ("FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| summarize FileOps=count(), DistinctFolders=dcount(FolderPath), Start=min(Timestamp), End=max(Timestamp), SampleFiles=make_set(FileName, 10)
         by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where FileOps > 2000 and DistinctFolders > 20   // empirical mass-encryption burst threshold
| order by FileOps desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where EventType in ("FileModified","FileRenamed","FileDeleted")
| summarize FileOps=count(), DistinctFolders=dcount(TargetFilePath), Start=min(TimeGenerated), End=max(TimeGenerated)
         by DvcHostname, ActingProcessId, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where FileOps > 2000 and DistinctFolders > 20   // mass-encryption burst threshold
| order by FileOps desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 -@Image:(*\System32\* OR *\system32\* OR *\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\*) -@Image:(*\MsMpEng.exe OR *\svchost.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName!=/\\(System32|SysWOW64)\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextProcessId, ContextImageFileName], function=count(as=FileOps))
| FileOps > 2000
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count as FileOps dc(Filesystem.file_path) as DistinctFiles min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.action=modified OR Filesystem.action=deleted OR Filesystem.action=created) by _time span=10m Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where FileOps > 2000 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - FileOps
| tstats summariesonly=false count as FileOps dc(Filesystem.file_path) as DistinctFiles min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.action=modified OR Filesystem.action=deleted OR Filesystem.action=created) by _time span=10m Filesystem.dest Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where FileOps > 2000 | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | sort - FileOps
Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest

| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

description: |

    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName

// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| order by TimeGenerated desc

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution

Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Adversary MFA method registration within 1h of a password reset (Scattered Spider / ShinyHunters ATO) · [LLM] MFA device registered from an IP never seen for the user (attacker enrollment for persistence)

Adversary MFA method registration within 1h of a password reset (Scattered Spider / ShinyHunters ATO) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the Scattered Spider / ShinyHunters account-takeover sequence the article's remediation section names: a help-desk-driven or self-service password reset immediately followed by the actor registering their own MFA authentication method/device on the same account. Correlates Entra ID audit reset events with security-info registration events on the same target within a tight window. Rationale: Uses the exact identity-plane TTP the article and Google/Mandiant hardening guidance name ('verify identity on password resets, device enrollment, and MFA changes') and CISA AA23-320A documents for Scattered Spider: reset password then transfer/register MFA to an attacker device. Correlating Entra reset + security-info-registration on one target inside 1h is high-fidelity because the two rarely fire back-to-back for the same principal in normal ops. Sentinel version keys on the true target (TargetResources); Defender CloudAppEvents version keys on AccountObjectId, best-covering the self-service-reset variant. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/expansion-shinyhunters-saas-data-theft • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/mandiant-finds-shinyhunters-using.html
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1556.006 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate help-desk password reset where the user then genuinely re-enrolls Authenticator on a newly issued phone
  • New-hire onboarding: initial credential set followed by first-time MFA registration
  • User lost/replaced phone, IT reset password and user re-registered device same session
  • Scheduled password-expiry rotation followed by prompted re-registration of security info
  • Bulk migration to a new MFA method (e.g. org-wide passkey rollout) driving many resets+registrations
Suppression filter
| where ResetIp !in ("<corp-egress-ranges-managed-elsewhere>") == false  // prefer: exclude registrations whose RegIp is in your corporate egress CIDR and ResetActor is a verified helpdesk service account
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the RegIp/ResetActor and check whether the reset was a verified, ticketed help-desk action; compare RegIp ASN/geo to the user's normal sign-in locations and confirm the newly registered method is one the user recognises. 2) Contain: if unverified, revoke the user's sessions/refresh tokens, remove the rogue authentication method, disable the account or force a verified re-registration, and block the RegIp. 3) Hunt: look for post-ATO activity on that principal — PowerShell/browser-driven mass downloads from SharePoint/OneDrive, new OAuth app consents, inbox-forwarding rules, and additional resets across other users from the same actor/IP.
let window = 1h;
let resets = CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType has_any ("Reset user password","Change user password","Reset password")
| project ResetTime = Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ResetIp = IPAddress, ResetAction = ActionType;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","registered all required security info")
| join kind=inner resets on AccountObjectId
| where Timestamp between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + window)
| project ResetTime, RegTime = Timestamp,
          DeltaMin = datetime_diff('minute', Timestamp, ResetTime),
          AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ResetAction, ResetIp, RegIp = IPAddress
| order by RegTime desc
let window = 1h;
let pwreset = AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("Reset password (by admin)","Reset user password","Change user password","Self-service password reset flow activity progress")
| where Result == "success"
| extend TargetId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id), TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| project ResetTime = TimeGenerated, ResetOp = OperationName, TargetId, TargetUpn,
          ResetActor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), ResetIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress);
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where OperationName in ("User registered security info","Admin registered security info","User registered all required security info","User started security info registration")
| where Result == "success"
| extend TargetId = tostring(TargetResources[0].id), TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName)
| project RegTime = TimeGenerated, RegOp = OperationName, TargetId, TargetUpn,
          RegActor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName), RegIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| join kind=inner pwreset on TargetId
| where RegTime between (ResetTime .. ResetTime + window)
| project ResetTime, RegTime, DeltaMin = datetime_diff('minute', RegTime, ResetTime),
          TargetUpn, ResetOp, ResetActor, ResetIp, RegOp, RegActor, RegIp
| order by RegTime desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:("User registered security info" OR "User registered all required security info" OR "Admin registered security info" OR "Reset user password" OR "Reset password (by admin)" OR "Change user password" OR "Self-service password reset flow activity progress")
CLOUD
sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Workload=AzureActiveDirectory (Operation="Reset user password" OR Operation="Change user password" OR Operation="Reset password (by admin)" OR Operation="Self-service password reset flow activity progress" OR Operation="User registered security info" OR Operation="User registered all required security info" OR Operation="Admin registered security info")
| eval target=coalesce(ObjectId,UserId)
| eval resetTime=if(match(Operation,"(?i)password"), _time, null())
| eval regTime=if(match(Operation,"(?i)registered security info"), _time, null())
| stats min(resetTime) as resetTime max(regTime) as regTime values(Operation) as ops values(ClientIP) as clientIPs by target
| where isnotnull(resetTime) AND isnotnull(regTime) AND regTime>=resetTime AND (regTime-resetTime)<=3600
| eval DeltaMin=round((regTime-resetTime)/60,1)
| convert ctime(resetTime) ctime(regTime)
| table target ops clientIPs resetTime regTime DeltaMin
| sort - regTime
MFA device registered from an IP never seen for the user (attacker enrollment for persistence) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the attacker-device MFA enrollment step from the same campaign, pivoting on infrastructure novelty instead of reset timing: an Entra security-info registration whose source IP has never appeared in that user's successful sign-in history over the baseline window. Surfaces enrollment from actor-controlled infrastructure after vishing/credential-harvesting SSO theft. Rationale: Second, distinct pivot on the same Mandiant/CISA-confirmed step (actor 'registered their own device for MFA'): novelty of the registration source IP against 30 days of the user's own successful sign-ins. This catches enrollment from attacker infrastructure even when no password-reset event preceded it (pure credential-harvesting/vishing path), which the timing-based UC would miss. Datadog is event-scoped only because per-user IP baselining must live in a rule-level reference table. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-320a • https://cloud.google.com/blog/topics/threat-intelligence/expansion-shinyhunters-saas-data-theft • https://thehackernews.com/2026/01/mandiant-finds-shinyhunters-using.html
ATT&CKT1098.005 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange.All_Changes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate remote/travelling user enrolling a new authenticator from a hotel/mobile-carrier IP not in baseline
  • New employee's first MFA registration (no prior sign-in baseline exists for the account)
  • User on a personal/home network never used for corporate sign-in registering a backup method
  • Corporate VPN or ZTNA egress change putting registration behind a new public IP/ASN
  • Consultant/contractor whose device connects from a client-site network for the first time
Suppression filter
| where RegActor !endswith "$"  // and, if available, exclude RegIp within corporate egress CIDR reference set
Response runbook
1) Triage: geo/ASN-enrich RegIp and confirm whether it belongs to the user's known networks or a hosting/VPN/mobile provider inconsistent with their profile; verify the registered method with the user out-of-band. 2) Contain: if unverified, revoke sessions and refresh tokens, delete the rogue authentication method, require verified re-registration, and add RegIp to conditional-access block. 3) Hunt: check the same RegIp/ASN for registrations against other users, subsequent SaaS data access (SharePoint/OneDrive downloads, Okta/SSO app access), and new OAuth grants or mailbox rules on the affected account.
let lookback = 30d;
let recent = 1d;
let baselineIPs = AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
| where ErrorCode == 0
| summarize by AccountObjectId, IPAddress;
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(recent)
| where ActionType has_any ("registered security info","registered all required security info")
| where isnotempty(IPAddress) and isnotempty(AccountObjectId)
| join kind=leftanti baselineIPs on AccountObjectId, IPAddress
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, ActionType, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP
| order by Timestamp desc
let lookback = 30d;
let recent = 1d;
let baselineIPs = SigninLogs
| where TimeGenerated between (ago(lookback) .. ago(recent))
| where ResultType == "0"
| summarize by UserPrincipalName, IPAddress;
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(recent)
| where OperationName in ("User registered security info","User registered all required security info","Admin registered security info")
| where Result == "success"
| extend TargetUpn = tostring(TargetResources[0].userPrincipalName), RegIp = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.ipAddress)
| where isnotempty(RegIp) and isnotempty(TargetUpn)
| join kind=leftanti (baselineIPs | project UserPrincipalName, IPAddress)
    on $left.TargetUpn == $right.UserPrincipalName, $left.RegIp == $right.IPAddress
| project TimeGenerated, TargetUpn, OperationName, RegIp,
          RegActor = tostring(InitiatedBy.user.userPrincipalName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:azure.activeDirectory @evt.name:("User registered security info" OR "User registered all required security info" OR "Admin registered security info")

sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Workload=AzureActiveDirectory (Operation="User registered security info" OR Operation="User registered all required security info")
| eval target=coalesce(ObjectId,UserId)

    search sourcetype="o365:management:activity" Workload=AzureActiveDirectory Operation="UserLoggedIn" earliest=-30d latest=-1d
    | eval target=coalesce(ObjectId,UserId)

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"

     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")

                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")

| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
